confirmed.title: syncOnce swallows IndexedDB failures from the push phase, so the status card can't tell them apart from a clean sync
confirmed.evidence: syncOnce (lib/sync/client.ts:154-181) wraps ONLY `pullChanges` in a try/catch that calls `setLastError` (lines 161-166); the `const push = await pushOutbox(options);` call on line 167 sits outside that catch, inside only the outer try/finally. drainOutbox (lib/sync/outbox.ts:306-334) itself only wraps the network call in its own try/catch (`try { response = await push(due.map(wireOp)); } catch (e) {...}` at lines 327-334) — everything before it (`await allOps()` at line 307, `await selectAndFreezeSettings(at)` at line 317, `capByBytes(...)` at line 320) runs unguarded. Every caller of syncOnce swallows the rejection generically: SyncBootstrap.tsx:19 `void syncOnce().catch(() => { /* Offline or signed out. */ })` and SyncStatus.tsx:136 `await syncOnce().catch(() => undefined);` — neither distinguishes 'offline' from 'a local IndexedDB call threw'.
confirmed.scenario: Any exception thrown by the pre-network IndexedDB work in a push pass — e.g. a QuotaExceededError writing the frozen settings op in selectAndFreezeSettings, or any other IDB hiccup while reading/writing the outbox or meta store — propagates out of drainOutbox → pushOutbox → straight past syncOnce's `setLastError` call (which only fires from the pullChanges catch block) and out through the outer try's `finally`. Every caller's blanket `.catch(() => …)` discards it without ever recording a last-error.
confirmed.impact: The SyncStatus card (components/SyncStatus.tsx) keeps showing whatever `lastError`/`lastSyncAt` it last had — 'Everything is sent' or a stale success timestamp — even though this sync pass failed outright before it ever reached the network, misrepresenting her data as safely synced when the outbox may in fact be stuck.
confirmed.fix: Wrap the whole `pushOutbox(options)` call in syncOnce in the same try/catch that already calls `setLastError(shortMessage(e))` for pullChanges (or add its own), so any pre-network throw inside drainOutbox is recorded as a real sync failure instead of being silently absorbed by the callers' generic `.catch()`.
confirmed.testGap: lib/sync/client.test.ts and lib/sync/outbox.test.ts test pullChanges/drainOutbox failure paths around the network push (`push` rejecting) but neither test drives a throw from allOps()/selectAndFreezeSettings()/capByBytes() ahead of the network call, so this asymmetric catch was never exercised.

confirmed.title: commitLogEntry swallows queue() rejection only structurally, not really
confirmed.evidence: async function commitLogEntry(...) { try { const res = await doFetch(...); if (res.status >= 500 || RETRY_STATUSES.has(res.status)) return queue(req); return (await res.json())...; } catch { return queue(req); } }  (lines 129-139); queue() calls `await enqueue(...)` -> `appendOp` -> `openSmcDb()`, which explicitly documents 'A rejected promise must not be cached, or one failed open wedges sync for the whole session' (lib/sync/idb.ts:41) and lets the open failure propagate. Verified empirically: `return innerAsyncCall()` inside a try (without `await`) does NOT get caught by the surrounding catch in Node/V8 — a script reproducing this exact shape (`return inner()` unawaited inside try/catch) resolved as REJECTED at the caller, bypassing the catch entirely.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha is offline or IndexedDB is unavailable (private browsing, storage quota hit, or a blocked DB upgrade — all real states on iOS Safari, the PWA's primary platform). She logs a food from the main 'Log a food' sheet. commitLogEntry's fetch fails (offline) -> `return queue(req)` is taken -> queue() calls enqueue() -> appendOp() -> openSmcDb() rejects. Because `return queue(req)` was never awaited, that rejection is NOT caught by commitLogEntry's own try/catch and propagates straight out of commitLogEntry as a rejected promise.
confirmed.impact: Three primary, daily-used call sites (`components/LogFoodSheet.tsx:328` confirmCatalogPortion, `components/ScanConfirmSheet.tsx:116` logIt, `components/CaptureSheet.tsx:190/241` commitAndReport/save via lib/capture-client.ts:245 commitDraft) all `await commitLogEntry(...)`/`commitDraft(...)` with no matching catch (LogFoodSheet has none at all; ScanConfirmSheet has only try/finally with no catch; CaptureSheet's save() has no try/catch either). In LogFoodSheet the food is already optimistically added to the visible day (`onAdd(entry)` at line 327, BEFORE the commit call) — so Sasha sees the meal logged on her Today screen while it was neither committed to the server NOR queued in the outbox: silent data loss on her core food-logging path, with an unhandled promise rejection as the only trace. In CaptureSheet, `setSaving(false)` never runs (no finally), leaving the Save button stuck in a saving state forever with no error message.
confirmed.fix: Await the returned promise before returning it inside both branches of commitLogEntry (`return await queue(req);` in both the try and catch bodies), or wrap queue(req) in its own try/catch that degrades to a clearly failed status instead of a silent local success. Then ensure every call site (LogFoodSheet.confirmCatalogPortion, ScanConfirmSheet.logIt, CaptureSheet.save/commitAndReport) catches the rejection and surfaces an error state instead of leaving an optimistic entry with no backing write.

CORRECTIONS:
1. The claimed scenario (Sasha offline → the `catch` branch at log-client.ts:138 executes `return queue(req)`) does NOT exercise the missing-await mechanism the finding centers on. That `queue(req)` call is already inside the terminal catch handler — there is no further catch for `await` to "unlock." Whether or not it is awaited, a rejection there propagates identically to the caller. The await/try-catch defect only actually matters for the *other* branch, log-client.ts:135 (5xx/retry-status response, not offline) — there the catch at 137-139 genuinely fails to catch a subsequent queue() rejection, exactly as reproduced. So the finding's chosen scenario doesn't demonstrate the bug it names; a real demonstration would need a 5xx/retryable response followed by a queue failure.
2. "Silent data loss" is not accurate for the flagged primary path. In LogFoodSheet, `onAdd(entry)` (page.tsx `logFood` → `addExtra`, lib/store.ts:193-196) writes the entry into the local `days` store synchronously, before commitLogEntry is even called. That write is not contingent on commitLogEntry succeeding, so the entry does not disappear from Sasha's own device/session — it stays visible in her Today view across reloads. What is actually lost, only in the narrow case where both the network call AND the local IndexedDB outbox write fail, is server sync (so no cross-device/backup copy) — a real but materially smaller harm than "data loss," and I found no evidence the legacy `lib/sync.ts` push provides a fallback here: `syncNow()` requires a legacy install-link token that the Phase 0 Supabase-Auth cutover retired, so it is effectively inert now.
3. The precondition is a double failure (transport failure or a 5xx AND an IndexedDB/outbox failure), not a single "she's offline" state — a normal offline log succeeds at `enqueue()` since that doesn't need network. This narrows real-world frequency versus the "critical, daily-used path" framing.

confirmed.title: Body-mass roll-up trusts the sample's unit is already kg without checking it
confirmed.scenario: The only guarantee that a health_samples row's value is in canonical units (kg for body_mass) is lib/health/units.ts's toCanonical(), called exclusively inside the ingest normalizers (lib/health/normalize.ts, lib/oura/map.ts). rollUpDay never re-checks a sample's unit field before treating value as already-canonical. The legacy migration writer (lib/migrate/legacy.ts:271-276) inserts historical weigh-ins straight into health_samples with unit: "lb" and the raw pounds value, bypassing toCanonical entirely (it isn't imported anywhere in legacy.ts). Any day carrying one of these rows renders body_mass_kg = day.weightLb verbatim - e.g. a 140 lb weigh-in shows as body_mass_kg: 140 instead of ~63.5 kg, a ~2.2x inflation.
confirmed.impact: This isn't just a display bug: lib/tdee.ts:82-85 (latestWeightKg) reads day.body_mass_kg straight off the daily rollup and feeds it into bmrMifflinStJeor(weightKg, ...) (line 47: 10 * weightKg + ...) to compute the BMR/TDEE lines Sasha sees on the Body dashboard. A 2.2x-too-high weight roughly doubles the displayed BMR/TDEE for any date whose weigh-in came from the legacy backfill (or any future write path that skips toCanonical), silently misleading her about her own energy needs with zero error surfaced anywhere in the pipeline.
confirmed.fix: Either (a) make rollUpDay defensive - call toCanonical(sample.type, sample.value, sample.unit) on every sample it rolls up (body_mass, and really every metric) so a non-canonical unit is caught and thrown/rejected rather than silently trusted, or (b) fix lib/migrate/legacy.ts to run the weigh-in value through toCanonical("body_mass", day.weightLb, "lb") before writing, and add a DB check constraint or migration backfill guard that only ever accepts the canonical unit per type in health_samples.

confirmed.title: Missed/late weekly-proposal cron permanently skips that week's check-in
confirmed.scenario: The Sunday 21:00-local cron invocation fails to run or errors before reaching writeProposal (Vercel outage, ESTIMATOR_ENABLED momentarily unset, a transient DB error, the global enforceRateLimit('jobs:weekly-proposal', 10, 3600) briefly saturated). Devin notices the next day (Monday/Tuesday) and re-triggers the endpoint by hand with the cron secret. asOf now resolves to Monday's date, so mondayOf(asOf) returns the CURRENT week's Monday, not the Sunday-just-passed week that actually needed a proposal. The job runs 'successfully' but computes and writes a proposal (or 'none') for the wrong week; the week whose Sunday check-in was missed never gets a proposal at all, silently and permanently — no error, no job_runs row, no alert names the gap.
confirmed.impact: Sasha relies on the Sunday proposal as her weekly opportunity to adjust calories/macros in step with her actual expenditure trend (weight loss/gain, training changes). A silently-skipped week means a week goes by with no chance to correct an outdated target, and nothing in the product — not Devin, not Sasha, not any log — ever surfaces that the check-in was missed rather than 'nothing warranted a change.'

confirmed.title: Spoofable X-Forwarded-For used as rate-limit key on ~11 routes
confirmed.evidence: app/api/log/propose/route.ts:22  `const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ?? "unknown"; await enforceRateLimit(`log:propose:ip:${ip}`, 30, 60);`. The same pattern (first hop of x-forwarded-for as the rate-limit key, applied BEFORE requireUser) appears in app/api/targets/route.ts:28, app/api/log/commit/route.ts:29, app/api/export/route.ts:165, app/api/expenditure/route.ts:12, app/api/proposals/route.ts:15, app/api/proposals/[id]/decide/route.ts:23, app/api/media/sign/route.ts:18, and lib/server/catalog.ts:68-72 (`clientIp`, shared by app/api/foods/search/route.ts, app/api/foods/barcode/route.ts, app/api/foods/[id]/route.ts). Contrast with app/auth/callback/route.ts:18-30, whose own comment explains why: "Vercel's edge network sets x-real-ip to the address it actually accepted the connection from and overwrites any client-supplied value, so it can be trusted. x-forwarded-for cannot: a caller can set it to anything, so keying the limiter on it lets an attacker rotate past enforceRateLimit entirely." That route uses `req.headers.get("x-real-ip")` instead. lib/server/catalog.test.ts:47-51 only tests that the first hop is parsed correctly, never that it resists spoofing.
confirmed.scenario: An unauthenticated caller sends repeated POST /api/log/propose (or /api/coach, /api/export, /api/media/sign, etc.) requests, setting a different `X-Forwarded-For: <random-ip>` header on every request. Because Vercel appends the real client IP after any client-supplied value rather than replacing it, `.split(",")[0]` always reads the attacker-controlled value, so each request lands in a fresh `enforceRateLimit` bucket and the pre-identity IP throttle (e.g. 30/60s on log:propose, 120/60s on coach:pre) never engages. The attacker can drive unlimited traffic into `requireUser()` (a live call to Supabase's auth/JWKS service) and into AI-call-adjacent routes, with no bound from the IP leg of the design's own two-layer (IP + user) rate limiting.
confirmed.impact: This defeats the pre-identity "flood brake" the codebase's own comments describe as load-bearing (e.g. coach route: "this first limiter is the pre-identity flood brake"; log/propose: "burst 30/min"). For a phone-first PWA serving one person, sustained spoofed-header flooding can drive up Supabase Auth/API cost or trip Supabase's own account-level throttling, degrading or blocking the app exactly when Sasha needs to log a meal or check her plan — and it undermines a control the team explicitly engineered correctly once (auth/callback) but did not carry to the other 8+ places that need it.
confirmed.fix: Replace `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]` with `req.headers.get("x-real-ip")` (falling back to a per-request unique key when absent, as app/auth/callback/route.ts:29-32 already does) in every route listed above, and in `clientIp()` in lib/server/catalog.ts so foods/search, foods/barcode and foods/[id] inherit the fix. Centralizing this as one shared helper (e.g. exported from lib/server/http.ts) would prevent the inconsistency from recurring.

All ~11 call sites use the identical spoofable-XFF pattern before requireUser(); the codebase's own auth/callback route documents the exact spoofability rationale and uses x-real-ip instead, so this is a genuine, internally-inconsistent security gap, not a misreading. I found no guard (middleware, vercel.json, WAF config in-repo) that neutralizes the scenario. However the claimed severity of "high" overstates impact for this app: (1) it is not an auth bypass — requireUser() and its own per-user rate limit still gate every route, matching the taxonomy's "critical = auth bypass" definition, which does not apply here; (2) the underlying limiter is already a documented Phase-0, single-instance, best-effort mechanism the team explicitly scoped to "enough for one user," so defeating its IP leg specifically removes a soft pre-identity throttle, not a hard control; (3) exploitation requires an external attacker to discover and deliberately flood a low-profile single-user PWA's API routes, which is a plausible but not a "main path" scenario, and the worst realistic outcomes (elevated Supabase Auth calls, Vercel invocation cost, transient availability degradation) don't fit the given "high" examples (wrong numbers, sync loss, silent failure on a main path). This is best classified as medium: a real, evidence-backed missing/degraded security control (spoofable rate-limit key, inconsistent with the codebase's own stated threat model) that is an edge case requiring active adversarial conditions rather than a defect Sasha would hit in normal use. The proposed fix (swap to x-real-ip with the callback route's own fallback pattern, centralize as a shared helper) is correct and minimal and should still be applied.

Reproduces exactly as described. Every cited location uses the identical spoofable pattern `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ?? I could not find any code-level control (WAF, captcha, additional limiter) that neutralizes this; any such protection would be Vercel/Supabase platform config outside this repo, unverifiable from the codebase. The finding is CONFIRMED, not refuted — but its severity is overstated against the rubric given. Bypassing this limiter does not bypass auth (requireUser still 401s every unauthenticated request) and causes no data loss or safety-rule violation, so it does not meet the "critical" bar; it also isn't "wrong numbers shown / sync loss / silent failure on a main path" under normal operation — it is a hardening gap that only matters if an attacker actively discovers and floods this specific, unadvertised single-user app's URL with spoofed headers, which is a plausible but not demonstrated real-world risk here (worst case is elevated Supabase Auth/Vercel invocation cost and possible availability degradation during a deliberate attack, not a broken main path for Sasha under ordinary use). That profile fits "medium" (a real, testable coverage/hardening gap with bounded, attack-dependent impact) better than "high."

confirmed.title: Legacy /api/sync push has no rate limit, no size cap, no schema validation
confirmed.evidence: app/api/sync/route.ts:12-26 — both GET and POST call only `bearerOk(req, "SASHA_SYNC_TOKEN")` and `isConfigured()`; there is no `enforceRateLimit` call anywhere in the file (every other route in the repo calls `enforceRateLimit` before or alongside identity — e.g. app/api/log/commit/route.ts:29-30, app/api/sync/ops/route.ts). POST also does `const body = (await req.json()) as PushBody;` (line 23) — an unchecked TypeScript cast, not a runtime `zod` parse — versus app/api/sync/ops/route.ts, which validates every op through `OpsRequestSchema`, and every other body-accepting route in the app, which goes through `readJson(req, schema, maxBytes)` (lib/server/http.ts:24-45) for both a size cap and zod validation. lib/server/db.ts:24-28 defines `PushBody` as a bare TS type with no corresponding schema. No app/api/sync/route.test.ts exists (confirmed absent) to guard any of this.
confirmed.scenario: AGENTS.md states this legacy sync path is still live in production alongside the new Supabase-auth path ("Phase 0 release A — legacy and new path both live"). Anyone holding SASHA_SYNC_TOKEN (or a buggy/looping client using it) can POST an arbitrarily large JSON body with any shape to /api/sync with no throttle: a malformed `days` entry that happens to satisfy `newer()` (e.g. missing fields `resolveDay` in lib/resolve.ts expects, or a `date` key that doesn't match its own `.date` field) is upserted straight into the `days` table via `pushRecords` (lib/server/db.ts:84-96) with no schema check, and a client that retries aggressively has no per-minute cap bounding how many writes land.
confirmed.impact: This is the store for Sasha's entire food list and daily meal history. A malformed or oversized push here risks corrupting `days`/`foods`/`settings` data with no server-side shape guard (unlike every other write path in the app), which is exactly the kind of "any date renders a complete day" guarantee AGENTS.md's own test-guarded rules depend on — a corrupted day record could silently break her plan rendering. It also has no defense-in-depth against a compromised or misbehaving client hammering writes.
confirmed.fix: Add `enforceRateLimit` (mirroring the pattern used by every cron job and every other authenticated route) and switch `(await req.json()) as PushBody` to `readJson(req, pushBodySchema, MAX_BYTES)` with a real zod schema for `PushBody`, matching the rigor already applied to the newer app/api/sync/ops path. Given this path is slated for retirement in release B, accelerating that cutover is an acceptable alternative to hardening code being deleted soon.

confirmed.title: CaptureSheet ignores saveDraft's own failure signal
confirmed.evidence: lib/capture/drafts.ts's saveDraft() is explicitly documented to return "ok" | "too_large" | "unavailable" so "a private-browsing failure is a return value, never a throw" (lines 8, 26-40). CaptureSheet.tsx's settle() calls it and drops the result: `if (outcome.kind === "draft") { saveDraft(outcome.draft); setDraft(outcome.draft); setMessage(null); return; }` (line 219) — no branch anywhere checks for "too_large" or "unavailable".
confirmed.scenario: Sasha photographs a meal in private browsing (or with a full storage quota after weeks of use). The propose call succeeds and the draft renders in the confirm sheet (React state), but saveDraft() returns "unavailable" and nothing is persisted to localStorage. If she backgrounds the app before tapping Log, or the sheet reopens after a 409 duplicate_request recovery (which reads back through latestDraft()), the draft is gone with no warning ever shown — `setMessage(null)` even actively clears any prior message.
confirmed.impact: A capture she took a photo for can silently vanish without her ever being told the save didn't take, forcing a redo she has no way to anticipate.
confirmed.fix: Branch on saveDraft()'s return value in settle(): when it is "too_large" or "unavailable", set a user-visible message (the file already has a `message` state slot used elsewhere) instead of silently continuing as if it persisted.

votes.reason:
Re-read confirms the claim exactly. lib/capture/drafts.ts:26-40 defines saveDraft() returning "ok"|"too_large"|"unavailable", with the docstring at line 8 stating a storage failure is a return value, never a throw. components/CaptureSheet.tsx:217-223 (settle(), the "draft" branch) calls `saveDraft(outcome.draft)` at line 219 and discards the result — no code path anywhere in the file, or anywhere else in the repo (grepped for saveDraft call sites), branches on "too_large" or "unavailable". `setMessage(null)` on line 221 actively clears any earlier message, so a storage failure produces zero user-visible signal at the moment it happens.

I traced the loss mechanics further than the finding did. Because app/page.tsx:604-611 mounts CaptureSheet with only `initialMode` (never `initialDraft`), and `loadDraft` is called nowhere in production code (only in tests/client/capture-drafts.test.ts), the persisted draft's only real runtime consumer is the in-session `latestDraft()` call in the "duplicate" branch (CaptureSheet.tsx:225). Working through that branch shows it is actually NOT a loss vector by itself: if the first propose response already reached the client, React state (`flow.draft`) already holds the draft regardless of whether the localStorage write succeeded, so a later 409/duplicate settle still shows the Confirm sheet correctly either way — the finding's second scenario clause ("or the sheet reopens after a 409 duplicate_request recovery") is weaker than it claims. But the primary scenario is real and unmitigated: component unmount from app backgrounding/reload before she taps Log, with saveDraft() having silently failed under private browsing or a full quota. Nothing rehydrates a pending draft on remount, so the capture vanishes with no message ever shown. No test guards this integration (tests/client/capture-drafts.test.ts only unit-tests drafts.ts in isolation; no CaptureSheet-level test exists for this path). The proposed fix — branch on saveDraft's return in settle() and set flow.message on failure — is minimal and correct.

confirmed.title: ProposalCard approve/reject has no error handling
confirmed.evidence: decide() (lines 37-45): `async function decide(decision) { setBusy(true); try { await decideProposalOnline(proposal.id, decision); onDecided(decision); } finally { setBusy(false); } }` — there is no catch. decideProposalOnline() (lib/estimator-client.ts lines 85-100) throws `new Error("Needs a connection")` when offline and `new Error(\`decide failed: ${res.status}\`)` on any non-2xx response.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha taps 'Use these' on the Today-screen target proposal card when the request fails (e.g. a transient 500, or the network drops mid-request while `navigator.onLine` still reads true). decideProposalOnline() throws; decide()'s try/finally has no catch, so the rejection propagates unhandled from the onClick handler. `busy` resets to false (button re-enables) but onDecided is never called and no message renders anywhere in the component.
confirmed.impact: She gets no feedback at all about whether her tap on 'Use these' / 'Keep mine' took effect — the card just sits there as if nothing happened, and the failure is only visible as an unhandled promise rejection in a console she has no reason to open. There is no ProposalCard test file to have caught this.
confirmed.fix: Add a catch in decide() that sets a local error message (mirroring the `offline` copy already rendered below the buttons) so a failed decide shows a retry-able error instead of silently doing nothing.

confirmed.title: Runtime SDK pin (assertPinnedSdk) is never called outside tests/canary
confirmed.evidence: `assertPinnedSdk` is defined at lib/ai/adapter.ts:37-44 and the adapter's own top-of-file comment claims "The installed SDK major is asserted for the same reason [as the model-id pin]: a major upgrade gets its own canary, deliberately." Grepping the whole repo, the only callers are scripts/ai-canary.ts:77 (a manual, off-CI script) and lib/ai/adapter.test.ts. `generateStructured` (the function every real request path — coach, capture, weekly review — goes through) only calls `installedGenai()` at line 293 to stamp `sdk_version` on the `ai_calls` row; it never calls `assertPinnedSdk()`, so a major-version mismatch is recorded but not blocked at runtime.
confirmed.scenario: The only actual enforcement of the SDK-major pin at build time is scripts/verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs (wired into `pnpm build`, run in CI's `build` job), which compares the installed `@google/genai` package.json against the hand-maintained lib/ai/sdk-version.json. If that build/CI step were ever skipped for a deploy (a manual `next build` without the full `pnpm build` script, or a deploy pipeline that only invokes `next build` directly), a `@google/genai` major bump installed via the `^2.21.0` caret range in package.json would ship to production with no runtime check to catch it — `generateStructured` would just start calling the new major's API shape unchecked.
confirmed.impact: Lower likelihood than the other findings (CI's `build` job does run `pnpm build`, and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` makes the installed version deterministic from the committed lockfile), but the code's own documentation claims a runtime assertion exists ("is asserted") when in practice all real request paths silently skip it. This is worth tightening since a version-drift surprise is explicitly the failure the pin exists to prevent, and today only a single, easily-bypassed build script stands between a mismatch and production.
confirmed.fix: Either call `assertPinnedSdk()` once at module load in lib/ai/adapter.ts (or lazily on the first `generateStructured` call) so a mismatched major fails fast at runtime too, or correct the adapter's doc comment to say the pin is enforced only at build time via scripts/verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs, not asserted per-call.
confirmed.testGap: lib/ai/adapter.test.ts tests assertPinnedSdk() as a pure function but has no test asserting generateStructured() calls it (or refuses to run on a mismatched major).

votes.reason: The finding's factual claims all check out: assertPinnedSdk is defined at lib/ai/adapter.ts:37-44, its only callers are scripts/ai-canary.ts:77 and lib/ai/adapter.test.ts, and generateStructured (lib/ai/adapter.ts:288-323, the path every real coach/capture/weekly-review call goes through) calls installedGenai() only to stamp sdk_version (line 293) and never calls assertPinnedSdk(). So the code is not "wrong" as described -- it genuinely is dead code outside tests/canary, and the top-of-file comment ("The installed SDK major is asserted...") does overclaim. However, a guard elsewhere already substantially covers the actual production-risk scenario the finding worries about, which the finding underweights: (1) lib/ai/adapter.test.ts's third assertPinnedSdk-block test ("returns the build-verified version embedded for runtime calls") calls the REAL installedGenai() and asserts installed.major === PINNED_GENAI_MAJOR using real values, not mocks -- this is exactly the sdk-version.json-vs-PINNED_GENAI_MAJOR drift check assertPinnedSdk exists for, and it runs in CI's required "quality" job (pnpm test) on every push/PR to main. (2) The build job (needs: quality) runs pnpm build = "next build && node scripts/verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs", which independently compares the actual installed node_modules manifest against lib/ai/sdk-version.json and exits 1 on mismatch. (3) package.json pins "@google/genai": "^2.21.0" and CI uses pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, so an accidental major bump cannot occur via routine install -- it requires a deliberate version-range edit, which the finding's own author already flags as lowering likelihood. (4) Even in the worst case, generateStructured already wraps every call in retries, a circuit breaker, and zod schema validation (the parsed.success check), so an unpinned major's API-shape change would very likely surface as a thrown/logged failure rather than a silent wrong answer, and it never touches the food-safety guards in lib/foods.ts that matter most for Sasha. Net: this is a real but low-impact dead-code/doc-accuracy issue (fix the comment, or wire assertPinnedSdk into the existing tested check for consistency), not a medium-severity production risk -- the failure mode it describes is already caught twice over in required CI before any deploy.

confirmed.title: Sheet has no focus trap or Escape-to-close
confirmed.evidence: components/Sheet.tsx:68 sets `role="dialog" aria-modal="true"` but nothing in the file (or in its main consumers, e.g. BuildMealSheet.tsx, LogFoodSheet.tsx) moves focus into the sheet on open, traps Tab within it, or listens for the Escape key to call `onClose` — confirmed by `grep -n 'Escape|keydown|focus()' components/Sheet.tsx components/BuildMealSheet.tsx components/LogFoodSheet.tsx` returning no matches.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha uses VoiceOver/keyboard-adjacent navigation (Switch Control, a Bluetooth keyboard, or a browser extension) to open any of the core logging sheets (Build a Meal, Log a food, Log a meal). Focus stays wherever it was before the sheet opened, Tab can reach controls behind the scrim, and there is no Escape shortcut to dismiss.
confirmed.impact: Assistive-tech users lose the standard dialog affordances (trapped focus, Escape to close) on every one of the app's core logging flows, which are the main daily interaction surface.
confirmed.fix: On mount, move focus to the sheet's first focusable element (or the close button) and restore focus to the trigger on close; add a `keydown` listener for Escape that calls `onClose`; trap Tab/Shift+Tab within the dialog while open.
confirmed.testGap: none

confirmed.title: ProposalCard swallows a stale-proposal 409 with no user feedback
confirmed.evidence: `decide()` (components/ProposalCard.tsx:37-45) awaits `decideProposalOnline` inside a try/finally with no catch. `decideProposalOnline` (lib/estimator-client.ts:85-100) throws `Error('decide failed: ${res.status}')` on any non-2xx response, including the 409 `ProposalConflictError` that `app/api/proposals/[id]/decide/route.ts:32-35` returns when the proposal she's viewing was already superseded or decided (e.g. by write_target_proposal auto-rejecting it when a newer Sunday proposal landed). `onDecided` is only called on success (line 41), so a thrown error leaves `pendingProposal` in app/page.tsx untouched and only resets `busy` via `finally`.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha opens the app with a pending proposal cached from a previous visit. Before she taps, the weekly-proposal cron fires again (or the estimate was decided on another device) and the DB-level `write_target_proposal`/`approve_target_proposal` logic correctly marks her cached proposal as no longer pending. She taps 'Use these'; the POST returns 409; the promise rejects; nothing is caught. She sees no error message, the card stays fully interactive, and she can keep tapping indefinitely with no explanation of why 'nothing happens'.
confirmed.impact: The server-side single-pending-proposal invariant is correctly enforced (no wrong target is ever silently applied), but the one person using this app is left with a dead, confusing UI element on a screen she checks daily, with no path to understanding that her decision didn't register.
confirmed.fix: Catch the rejection in `decide()`, surface a message (e.g. 'This proposal changed — reload to see the latest'), and clear/refresh `pendingProposal` from the server on a 409 instead of leaving the stale card mounted.

confirmed.title: job_runs 'running' lock has no reaper — a crashed weekly-proposal run blocks all retries for that week
confirmed.evidence: `takeLock` (app/api/jobs/estimate/route.ts:60-68, reused by app/api/jobs/weekly-proposal/route.ts:23) inserts a `job_runs` row with `status: 'running'` and treats a unique-constraint violation (23505) as 'already locked'. `releaseLock` (lines 70-77) is only ever invoked from the handler's own try/catch (app/api/jobs/weekly-proposal/route.ts:76-89) — there is no TTL, no reaper, and no other code path anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn job_runs`) that ever flips a stuck 'running' row back to a retryable state.
confirmed.scenario: The weekly-proposal serverless function is killed mid-run (Vercel function timeout, deploy interrupting the request, OOM) after `takeLock` inserts the ('weekly-proposal', userId, weekStart) row but before `releaseLock` runs. The `job_runs` primary key (job, user_id, run_key) permanently blocks every later invocation for that same week — including a deliberate manual retry — because `takeLock` always sees the existing 'running' row and returns false, incrementing `out.skipped` with no error surfaced.
confirmed.impact: A single mid-flight crash silently prevents Sasha's Sunday proposal (and, via the same pattern, the nightly `estimate` job and `weekly-review`) from ever being generated for the rest of that week, with no automatic recovery and no alert — she simply gets no card that week and nothing in the response tells anyone why, since a 'skipped' lock looks identical to 'proposal already exists, correctly deduped'.
confirmed.fix: Add an age check to `takeLock` (e.g. treat a 'running' row older than the function's max duration as reclaimable and allow a new attempt to overwrite it), or a separate reaper cron that marks stale 'running' rows as 'error' so the per-week lock cannot wedge indefinitely.
confirmed.testGap: none found — no test simulates a crash between takeLock and releaseLock for weekly-proposal or estimate.

A repo-wide grep for job_runs and for stale/reap/TTL/stuck/force-unlock/clear-lock found zero reaper, cron, trigger, or admin path that ever updates a stuck running row. The job_runs PK (job, user_id, run_key) in the migration has no expiry column, so any pre-existing row (crashed or not) blocks re-insertion via 23505, and the {ran,skipped,errors} response genuinely can't distinguish a stuck lock from correct dedup. The scenario, mechanism, and severity (confined to one week's proposal, no data loss, no safety-rule impact, so medium not high/critical) all check out against the actual code.

confirmed.title: Offline scan-cache always downgrades a blocked verdict to a generic 'unverified' warning
confirmed.scenario: Sasha scans a product online; the server correctly returns verdict: 'blocked', reason: 'allergen:gluten', and the item is cached via rememberScan for offline reuse. Later, offline (e.g. in a store with no signal), she rescans the same barcode. scanGtin throws ScanUnavailable, BarcodeScanSheet falls back to resolveOffline + offlineMatch (lib/barcode/client.ts:66-69), which unconditionally returns policy: { verdict: 'unverified' } -- the specific 'Contains gluten' alert badge she saw online is silently replaced by the generic amber 'No ingredient list -- check the pack' message, discarding the fact the product was already known-bad.
confirmed.impact: The offline path is specifically meant to help her when the signal path guards work already (a repeat scan resolving from the phone), but it loses the strongest safety signal (an explicit blocked/'Contains X' alert) exactly in the scenario it's supposed to serve -- a rescan of a product she may already know is off-plan. Since the app's own design ('marking, never hiding') never blocks logging either way, the badge text is the only signal she gets, and this degrades it.
confirmed.testGap: tests/barcode/scan-cache.test.ts and tests/barcode/client.test.ts were not inspected for this specific offline-verdict-preservation case; there is no test asserting that a cached 'blocked' match still shows as blocked offline (the offlineMatch implementation hardcodes 'unverified' unconditionally, so such a test would currently fail).
confirmed.fix: Persist enough of the online BarcodeMatch (at minimum allergenTags and the policy verdict/reason, not just nutrition data) into CachedRevision so offlineMatch can reconstruct the real verdict instead of always returning 'unverified'. At minimum, recompute evaluatePolicy client-side from the cached allergenTags against her last-synced constraint profile rather than discarding the information entirely.

confirmed.title: kind=weight export still paginates by offset with no tie-breaker column
confirmed.evidence: let query = client.from(source.from).select(source.select).order(source.order, { ascending: true }).range(from, from + PAGE_SIZE); — for kind=weight, source.order is "start_time" alone (SOURCES.weight, line 52), with no secondary unique key. This is the one live kind still on the pre-Phase-2 offset scheme (kind=meals in the same SOURCES map is dead code in practice, since `STREAMED.has("meals")` is true and the streamed branch returns first at line 174, before SOURCES is ever consulted for it). Every migrated kind explicitly moved away from this: lib/server/export.ts:6-9 states 'Paging is keyset over (local_date, eaten_at, id), not offset, so a 12,000-row log exports with no gap and no duplicate.' No test exercises kind=weight with more than zero rows (tests/export/streams.test.ts:139-149 only asserts the empty case).
confirmed.scenario: If two weigh-ins ever land on the exact same `start_time` (duplicate import, clock-quantized entries, or simply enough history to cross a 1000-row page boundary at a tie), Postgres's ORDER BY on a non-unique column gives no guaranteed stable order across two separate `.range()` calls, so a row at the boundary can be duplicated or dropped between page N and page N+1.
confirmed.impact: Low likelihood (weight is logged at most a few times a day and rarely at identical timestamps) but the failure mode — a silently skipped or duplicated weigh-in row in an exported/backed-up dataset — is exactly the class of bug the newer keyset design was built to eliminate everywhere else.
confirmed.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (e.g. `id`) to the ORDER BY for the weight kind, or fold kind=weight into the same keyset-cursor pattern the other export kinds already use.

confirmed.title: Water tap has no error handling; failed write is silent
confirmed.scenario: Sasha taps 'Log water' from the FAB quick actions (a habit-tracking action she uses many times a day). IndexedDB is unavailable or the write throws — e.g. Safari private mode, storage quota exceeded, or a blocked/expired DB connection after the tab sat backgrounded — so `getRow`/`putRow` rejects. `addCups` rejects, `logWater`'s `await` throws before reaching `setWaterTick`/`refresh()`, and because it is invoked as `void logWater()` the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection: no toast, no retry, the water ring silently does not move, and nothing tells her the tap did nothing.
confirmed.impact: A core, high-frequency daily action (she is tracking hydration on a UC / fasting regimen) can fail with zero feedback. She has no way to know whether a tap registered; if it silently failed she will under-report water for the day with no way to notice or correct it.
confirmed.fix: Wrap the `onLogWater` handler (or `addCups` itself) in try/catch and surface a short inline error (matching the pattern already used for sync errors in lib/sync/client.ts's `shortMessage`), so a failed water write is visible and retryable instead of vanishing.
confirmed.testGap: none — no lib/water-client.test.ts exists for this function's failure path

votes.reason: Every claim in the finding checks out against the actual code. addCups (lib/water-client.ts:32-39) has no try/catch and calls getRow/putRow (lib/sync/idb.ts:75-80), which go through openSmcDb() — a promise explicitly NOT cached on rejection (idb.ts:44-46: 'dbPromise = null; throw e;'), so any IndexedDB failure (quota, blocked version-change, connection closed) propagates as a rejected promise on every call, not just the first. logWater (app/page.tsx:329-333) awaits addCups with no try/catch, so a rejection throws before reaching setWaterTick/refresh() — the ring genuinely does not move. It's invoked from an onClick with no .catch (components/QuickActions.tsx:145-150) and wired as `() => void logWater()` (app/page.tsx:666). Grepped the whole app/ and components/ tree: no unhandledrejection listener, no error.tsx/global-error.tsx, no ErrorBoundary anywhere. shortMessage (lib/sync/client.ts:131) is real but is wired only into the background outbox push-sync loop (client.ts:164), never into local read/write paths like addCups — the finding's contrast (the error-surfacing pattern already exists for sync, but isn't reused here) is accurate. I also checked whether some broader existing pattern makes the specific water claim moot: it does not — the other quick-action handlers (logFood, logGut, logWeight, addExtra/updateDay) are synchronous localStorage writes via lib/store.ts, not async IndexedDB writes, so addCups is the one quick-action call in this flow that is genuinely await-able-to-reject in a way that produces a silent unhandled-rejection with zero UI feedback. The proposed fix (wrap the handler, surface a short inline error reusing the shortMessage pattern) is minimal and appropriate. I lowered severity from medium to... actually keeping medium: the failure requires an actual IndexedDB exception (quota/version-change/security error), which is uncommon in a home-screen-installed iOS PWA (the app's primary use context per AGENTS.md) even though it is a real, unguarded gap; that likelihood, plus the fact it affects one quick-action among several with the same underlying gap, keeps it out of 'high' (wrong numbers already shown / sync loss / main-path failure that happens routinely) territory, but it is a genuine, reproducible correctness gap worth fixing as stated.
votes.evidence: lib/water-client.ts:32-39 (no try/catch in addCups); lib/sync/idb.ts:44-46 (rejected dbPromise not cached, so every call can re-throw) and idb.ts:75-80 (putRow/getRow have no error handling); app/page.tsx:329-333 (logWater awaits addCups with no try/catch; setWaterTick/refresh unreachable on throw); app/page.tsx:666 (`onLogWater={() => void logWater()}`, no .catch); components/QuickActions.tsx:145-150 (onClick calls onLogWater() with no catch); grep for 'unhandledrejection' and for ErrorBoundary/error.tsx across app/ and components/ returned nothing; lib/sync/client.ts:131,164 shows shortMessage wired only into the background sync-push loop, not any local write path; app/page.tsx:4 and lib/store.ts:184-203 show the other quick-action handlers (logGut/logWeight/addExtra/updateDay) are synchronous localStorage writes, distinguishing addCups as the one genuinely rejectable async call in this flow.

confirmed.title: Favorites strip vanishes silently on an IndexedDB read failure
confirmed.scenario: FavoritesStrip is rendered inside LogFoodSheet (the default 'Log food' flow) to give one-tap access to her frequently-eaten foods. If the IndexedDB read throws (blocked connection, private browsing, quota issue — same failure class as the water write above), `listFavorites()` rejects as an unhandled promise rejection, `rows` never updates from its initial `[]`, and the component's own guard `if (rows.length === 0) return null` makes the whole strip disappear with no error, no retry link, and no visual difference from 'she has no favorites yet'.
confirmed.impact: The fast-logging shortcut for her curated safe-food list silently stops working, pushing her into full search for foods she should be able to log with one tap; because the empty state and the failure state render identically, she cannot tell the difference or take a corrective action.
confirmed.fix: Catch the rejection and distinguish 'no favorites' from 'failed to load favorites' (e.g. keep the previous `rows` on error, or render a small retry affordance instead of returning null).
confirmed.testGap: none — no test file exists for FavoritesStrip or listFavorites' failure path

votes.reason: The chain is confirmed unguarded end to end. components/FavoritesStrip.tsx:24-28 calls `listFavorites().then(...)` with no `.catch`. lib/favorites-client.ts:70-89 `listFavorites()` calls `readIndex()` (line 71, itself `openSmcDb().get(...)` at line 28) and `allRows()` (line 74, `openSmcDb().getAll(...)` at lib/sync/idb.ts:84-86) with no try/catch anywhere in that call graph, so a rejected IndexedDB open/read propagates out of `listFavorites()` as an unhandled rejection and `setRows` never fires. The real production usage confirms the failure surface: components/LogFoodSheet.tsx:705 renders `<FavoritesStrip onPick={handleFavoritePick} />` with no `initial` prop, so `rows` starts at `useState<FavoriteRow[]>(initial ?? [])` = `[]` (FavoritesStrip.tsx:21), and on a rejected promise it stays `[]` forever, hitting `if (rows.length === 0) return null` (line 30) — visually identical to the legitimate 'no favorites yet' state. I found no error boundary (no app/error.tsx or global-error.tsx besides layout.tsx), no window-level unhandledrejection handler, and no retry/backoff logic anywhere in the chain (openSmcDb only nulls its cached promise on failure, lib/sync/idb.ts:56-60, so a later successful mount would retry, but this mount gets nothing). tests/favorites/favorites-strip.test.tsx only covers the empty-`initial`-array and populated-`initial`-array render paths, never the rejected-promise path, so no existing test guards this hole. The scenario (IndexedDB failing — private browsing, blocked connection, quota) is realistic for a phone-first PWA. Severity as medium is appropriate: this degrades a convenience shortcut inside LogFoodSheet, not the underlying ability to log food (search still works), so it doesn't meet the 'silent failure on a main path' bar for high, but it is a genuine, evidenced, uncovered silent-failure bug.

votes.reason: Every mechanical claim in the finding checks out against the actual code, and I reproduced the exact failure mechanics in isolation. FavoritesStrip.tsx:24-28 calls `void listFavorites().then((next) => { if (live) setRows(next); })` with no `.catch()`. listFavorites() (lib/favorites-client.ts:70-89) awaits readIndex() -> openSmcDb().get(), allRows() -> openSmcDb().getAll(), and getRow('recipes', id) -> openSmcDb().get() (all in lib/sync/idb.ts), none wrapped in try/catch anywhere in the chain. A rejection from any of these (IndexedDB blocked/quota/private-mode/corrupted) therefore becomes an unhandled promise rejection, `rows` state never updates from its initial `[]` (FavoritesStrip is invoked with no `initial` prop at its real call site, components/LogFoodSheet.tsx:705), and `if (rows.length === 0) return null` (FavoritesStrip.tsx:30) renders nothing. confirmed.title: Bundled-catalog search misses plain plural queries like "eggs"
confirmed.evidence: scoreName() only awards points when a query token is an exact word match, a prefix of a DB word, a substring of the joined name, or a subsequence of a DB word (which by construction requires the query to be no longer than the word it matches against) — a query token longer than every candidate word can never score. Confirmed by running the exact scoreName/tokens/subsequence code against the real lib/food-db.json rows: scoreName(tokens("eggs"), "Egg, whole, large") === 0, scoreName(tokens("eggs"), "Egg, hard-boiled") === 0, scoreName(tokens("eggs"), "Egg white") === 0, while scoreName(tokens("egg"), ...) scores 985-991. All ten USDA egg rows in food-db.json are named singular ("Egg, whole, large", "Egg white", "Egg roll", etc.) with no row containing the substring "eggs".
confirmed.scenario: Offline (or with the catalog unavailable), she types the natural plural "eggs" into the search box — the same word her own preset food is literally named ("Eggs, large", lib/foods.ts:74, which IS found because it is stored as 'eggs' verbatim) — but if that food is not already in her `mine` list, or she is looking for a specific USDA prep like "Egg, hard-boiled", the entire bundled USDA egg category returns zero hits, with CatalogSearch.tsx showing "Nothing matches. Try fewer words, or type it from the label below."
confirmed.impact: This is a general class of miss (any USDA/bundled row whose word is singular while she types the natural plural) affecting one of the most commonly logged proteins in her plan, and it is silent — she gets no hits and no indication that the food exists under a different form of the word, so she is nudged toward the manual "type it from the label" flow for a food that's already curated in the database.
confirmed.fix: Add a simple stem/plural-strip step before matching (e.g. try the query with a trailing 's' or 'es' removed as an additional candidate token) or fall back to a shorter subsequence check when the query is a simple plural of a DB word.

confirmed.title: Provider circuit breaker is per-instance in-memory state on a serverless deployment
confirmed.evidence: `const failures = new Map<string, number[]>();` (lib/ai/circuit.ts:10) is module-level, in-process state; the file's own comment says so explicitly: "Module-level, per instance: `failures` maps provider → failure timestamps... five failures in ten minutes open the circuit." `assertCircuitClosed`/`recordFailure` only ever read/write this in-memory map — there is no database or KV-backed counter. app/api/coach/route.ts and the other AI-calling routes run with `export const runtime = "nodejs"` on Vercel (per AGENTS.md, Vercel Git integration builds production from main), where Next.js API routes execute as independent serverless function instances that can cold-start on any request.
confirmed.scenario: Gemini has a bad stretch (the kind docs/ai-data-handling.md itself records happening on 2026-09-13, where 3.8 and 3.7 exhausted retries with 503 before the pin moved to 3.6). Each of Sasha's coach turns or capture calls that lands on a fresh/cold serverless instance starts `recentFailureCount('google')` back at 0, so the 5-failures-in-10-minutes threshold in `assertCircuitClosed` (circuit.ts:25-33) may never actually accumulate across instances even though the provider is genuinely failing repeatedly for her.
confirmed.impact: The circuit breaker's purpose — stop hammering (and paying for retries against) a sick provider once it's shown a failure pattern — can silently not engage in production, because the failure count it depends on resets on every cold start instead of accumulating per-user/per-deployment the way the daily spend cap and turn budget were deliberately redesigned to do (assertTurnBudget in lib/server/coach.ts:71-73 explicitly notes "a serverless cold start forgets a Map" as the reason it counts from `ai_calls` instead — the same reasoning was not applied to the circuit breaker).
confirmed.fix: Back the circuit breaker's failure counter with the same durable store used for the spend cap and turn budget (a recent-failures query against `ai_calls`, or a small dedicated table/KV entry), the same way lib/server/coach.ts already does for `assertTurnBudget`, instead of a module-level Map that a serverless cold start clears.

votes.reason: Every factual claim in the finding checks out against the actual code. lib/ai/circuit.ts:10 is a bare module-level `const failures = new Map<string, number[]>()`; assertCircuitClosed (lines 25-33) and recordFailure (lines 35-39) only ever read/write that map — no DB, no KV, nothing durable. It is wired into the single choke point for every provider call: lib/ai/adapter.ts:10-11 imports it, line 298 calls assertCircuitClosed(provider) and line 322 calls recordFailure(provider) inside generateStructured, which lib/server/coach.ts, lib/coach/turn.ts, lib/coach/weekly-review.ts and lib/ai/capture.ts all funnel through. The AI-calling routes (app/api/coach/route.ts:15, app/api/log/propose/route.ts:15, app/api/log/commit/route.ts:16, the jobs/* routes, etc.) are all `export const runtime = "nodejs"`, i.e. ordinary Vercel serverless functions subject to cold starts — and since each Next.js API route bundles into its own function, the map isn't even shared across routes that call the same provider, which is an even weaker form of the same gap than the finding states. The parallel the finding draws is exact and verified: lib/server/coach.ts:70-73 has the identical reasoning in a comment — "a serverless cold start forgets a Map, and '60 a day' has to survive one" — as the explicit reason assertTurnBudget reads from `ai_calls` instead of an in-memory counter, and that durability pattern was not applied to circuit.ts. adapter.test.ts:143-156 only exercises in-process accumulation via `__resetCircuit()`; there is no test (and none plausible in a unit suite) that proves the counter survives across separate serverless instances, so "missing coverage" also holds. One mitigating nuance: adapter.ts:82-88's own comment frames the circuit breaker as "the backstop for a sick database" (i.e., deliberately DB-independent so it still works when the spend-cap's `ai_calls` read itself fails), and per-call retries are already bounded (RETRIES=2, BACKOFF_MS=[250,1000], so 3 attempts max) and daily spend/turn volume are separately capped through durable `ai_calls` reads (assertUnderSpendCap, assertTurnBudget) — so a non-tripping circuit does not translate into unbounded cost or an unbounded hammering loop, only into extra per-turn retry latency during a real provider outage. That tempers "impact" language like "silently not engage" but does not make the underlying claim false: the circuit's specific 5-failures-in-10-minutes fast-fail behavior genuinely may not engage across cold starts, exactly as described, and the fix direction (a durable failure counter) is a legitimate one even if the ai_calls table specifically is an imperfect choice given the "backstop for a sick database" intent. This is squarely the described medium bucket: a real edge case, a real (if modest) UX/cost degradation, and a real coverage gap — not a critical/high issue since it never touches Sasha's core offline meal-plan, food-safety, or logging paths, all of which work without any AI call at all.

Two pieces of internal evidence make this more than speculative: (1) lib/server/coach.ts:70-73 contains the team's own prior fix of the identical bug class for the turn budget — the comment reads "The budget is counted from ai_calls, not from the in-memory limiter: a serverless cold start forgets a Map" — proving the team already diagnosed and fixed this exact failure mode elsewhere in the same file family. (2) docs/plans/2026-09-10-phase-0/lane-D-data-ops.md:1293 shows the `ai_calls.status`/`error` columns were added specifically "so the circuit breaker's history is auditable" — i.e. the durable substrate for a cross-instance circuit breaker already exists and was intentionally built for this purpose, but `assertCircuitClosed`/`recordFailure` never query it. votes.reason:
The technical claim is accurate (lib/ai/circuit.ts:10, confirmed by its own comment) but the impact claim does not hold up. Two things neutralize it for Sasha specifically:

1. The circuit breaker is purely a fail-fast/cost-efficiency optimization, not a correctness or safety gate. Whether or not it opens, a real provider outage produces the exact same user-visible outcome: generateStructured (lib/ai/adapter.ts:288-334) always attempts up to RETRIES+1=3 calls with backoff and, on exhaustion, calls recordFailure then rethrows the provider's own error (adapter.ts:322-325), which propagates as a surfaced HttpError/failed turn — never silently. If the circuit is open instead, assertCircuitClosed throws immediately (circuit.ts:25-33), one call earlier, with a slightly different message. Either way Sasha sees a failed coach turn / capture; nothing about food data, macro numbers, or logged history is wrong or lost in either branch.

2. The financial/abuse protection this finding worries about ("stop hammering (and paying for retries against) a sick provider") is a non-issue here: aiCallRow sets cost_estimate to 0 on any failed call (adapter.ts: `cost_estimate: result ? estimateCostUsd(...) : 0`), and the durable, cold-start-proof protections already exist independently — assertUnderSpendCap reads summed cost from `ai_calls` (adapter.ts:82-103) and assertTurnBudget reads counts from `ai_calls` (lib/server/coach.ts:71-89, explicitly for the cold-start reason the finding cites). A non-functioning circuit breaker cannot blow the spend cap (failed calls cost $0) or bypass the turn budget (it only counts successful calls anyway). The worst realistic consequence is a few hundred extra ms of retry latency per call and a handful of extra requests to a struggling Gemini endpoint during an outage — not data loss, not a safety-rule breach (gluten/dairy/apple exclusion is unrelated to this code path), not auth bypass, and not "wrong numbers shown" since a failed AI call never writes menu/macro data at all.

Per the impact lens, this has no realistic path to wrong food, wrong numbers, lost data, or unauthorized access for a single-user phone-first PWA, so it is refuted as a real finding at the claimed medium severity. It remains a legitimate, low-priority resilience/cost-hygiene nit (worth noting, not worth prioritizing) — the fix suggested (back it with `ai_calls`, mirroring assertTurnBudget) is reasonable if someone wants to polish this, but nothing breaks for Sasha today because of it.

confirmed.title: Lint CI step cannot fail — eslint-config-next rules are warn-level, no --max-warnings
confirmed.evidence: ci.yml:30 runs `pnpm lint`, and package.json:9 defines `"lint": "eslint"` with no `--max-warnings` flag. eslint.config.mjs (repo root) is just `[...nextVitals, ...nextTs]` plus a globalIgnores block — it adds no custom `rules` section, so every rule keeps eslint-config-next's own severity. Running `pnpm lint` on HEAD today (verified in the scratchpad) prints `✖ 11 problems (0 errors, 11 warnings)` and exits 0 — e.g. app/api/constraints/route.ts:3 `'HttpError' is defined but never used`, and lib/health-client.ts:86 `Do not use window.location.assign() ... @next/next/no-location-assign-relative-destination` (a real full-page-reload bug risk for a PWA). Both are only warnings, so CI is green.
confirmed.scenario: A PR introduces any eslint-config-next warning-level issue — an unused import, a missing hook dependency (react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is warn in this preset), or another window.location.assign() instead of the router — anywhere in the diff. `eslint` exits 0 because it has zero *errors*, `pnpm lint` exits 0, the Lint step is green, and the PR merges with the regression unreviewed.
confirmed.impact: For Sasha's one-person PWA, this specific rule (no-location-assign) flags exactly the kind of bug that silently breaks the app-shell/offline experience (a hard navigation instead of a client-side route change can drop in-flight sync/outbox state); nothing in CI can ever catch it or its siblings because the lint gate has no enforceable threshold.
confirmed.fix: Add `--max-warnings 0` to the lint script (`"lint": "eslint --max-warnings 0"`), or promote the rules that matter (no-location-assign-relative-destination, no-unused-vars, react-hooks/exhaustive-deps) to "error" in eslint.config.mjs. Then fix (or explicitly allow) the 11 current warnings so the tightened gate starts green.

confirmed.title: Failed coach turn leaves a permanent ghost 'sending' bubble
confirmed.scenario: Sasha asks the coach 'can I eat X', the request 429s or 503s (budget cap, both providers down). `nextChatState` dispatches `{type:'error', ...}`, which clears `typing` and sets an error caption below the transcript, but the faded (`opacity: pending ? 0.6 : 1`, components/CoachMessage.tsx:19) bubble for her question stays in `state.messages` forever, still marked pending. If she taps 'Try again' (`onRetry={() => send(state.pendingText)}`, line 184), `send` mints a brand-new `messageId` and pushes a second pending bubble — the first stays orphaned until some future turn happens to succeed (the "turn" case blanket-filters `!m.pending`, not by id).
confirmed.impact: She cannot tell whether her question was ever sent; the UI shows a permanently 'in flight' message next to an error line, and a retry visibly duplicates her question rather than resending it in place — confusing in a screen she may use to check whether a food is safe to eat.
confirmed.fix: In the "error" case, mark or remove the specific pending message (match by the `messageId` the failed `send` used) instead of leaving it untouched, so the bubble reflects failure and a retry replaces it rather than adding a second one.
confirmed.testGap: none — no reducer test in this repo asserts on `state.messages` after an "error" event

The `ChatEvent` "error" variant (line 32) carries no `messageId`, and `send()`'s catch block (149-154) never passes the `messageId` it has in closure scope, so there is no way for the reducer to target the specific failed message even if it wanted to. Clicking "Try again" calls `send(state.pendingText)` (line 184), which mints a brand-new UUID and unconditionally appends a second pending bubble (52-59) — nothing dedupes by id or content, and nothing guards against retrying while a stale pending message exists. Both bubbles then coexist and render (keyed by distinct `m.id`, both opacity 0.6) until some future "turn" succeeds, since that case strips *every* `pending` message regardless of id (line 66: `!ids.has(m.id) && !m.pending`), exactly as the finding describes — confirming the duplicate is transient-but-real, not literally permanent, which the finding's own body already caveats correctly (only the title overstates "permanent"). Repeated failures compound this: each failed retry stacks one more orphaned pending bubble. tests/coach/chat-state.test.ts's "error" case (lines 30-37) checks only retryable/pendingText/typing, never messages, so this is a genuine, untested hole, not something an existing guard already covers. The proposed fix (thread the messageId onto the error event and mark/remove that specific message) is minimal and directly addresses the root cause. Impact is UI confusion during a network hiccup — no data loss, no wrong nutrition numbers, no safety-rule breach, self-heals on the next successful turn or page reload (restore overwrites local state) — which matches the stated "medium: edge case, degraded UX" bucket precisely, not high or low.

confirmed.title: Failed targets fetch is indistinguishable from 'nothing to show'
confirmed.scenario: Settings mounts and calls `void fetchTargets().then((result) => setTargets(result))` (app/settings/page.tsx:184). Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx response (e.g. a transient 500, or she opens Settings the instant she loses signal) resolves to `null` exactly like a legitimate 'no active targets yet' state — the same value the initial `useState<TargetsResponse | null>(null)` (line 153) already holds before the fetch even starts.
confirmed.impact: `canOpenTargetsSheet(targets)` (line 357 of app/settings/page.tsx) disables the calorie/protein target editor with no distinction between 'still loading', 'genuinely has no targets', and 'the request failed' — she sees a permanently greyed-out control with zero explanation and no retry. Unlike the sibling `fetchDaily`/`fetchCached` paths in the same file, which explicitly track offline/disabled/error state, this one collapses every failure into the same disabled UI.
confirmed.fix: Track load state separately from the value (e.g. `{status: 'loading'|'ready'|'error', value}` the way `useBodyProfile`/`fetchDaily` already do elsewhere in this codebase) and show a retry affordance or error caption when the fetch failed rather than reusing the empty-state disabled control.

The effect at app/settings/page.tsx:182-188 fires fetchTargets() exactly once on mount with no retry/online-listener anywhere in the file (grepped, none found), so a failure is sticky for the life of that mount. canOpenTargetsSheet (lib/estimator-client.ts:164-166) is targets !== null, and it gates a reachable control: the button at app/settings/page.tsx:351-361 renders whenever `visible` (the estimate) is truthy — which fetchExpenditure can satisfy from a stale localStorage cache even while the sibling fetchTargets call fails outright (fetchExpenditure uses fetchCached, which falls back to cache; fetchTargets has no such fallback) — so the disabled-with-no-explanation button is a genuinely reachable state, not just theoretical. There is no toast/error-boundary system in the app (grepped) to surface the failure another way. Confirmed by contrast: lib/health-client.ts:44-62 (fetchDaily) explicitly tracks {offline, disabled} and shows an 'offline, last synced copy' caption for the same class of failure — the asymmetry the finding cites is real. But that test only pins the boolean; it does not cover (and so does not guard against) the actual gap the finding identifies — no loading/error distinction, no retry affordance, no message — so the hole survives the existing guard. Also worth noting: this whole path sits behind NEXT_PUBLIC_ESTIMATOR_UI, whose production on/off state isn't verifiable from the repo (docs/readiness/2026-09-12-production-readiness.md:102 says 'not determinable from routes alone'; docs/plans/2026-09-12-bug-batch-spec.md:250 lists setting it in Vercel production as a still-pending ops step) — this bounds current real-world exposure but does not change whether the code is correct.

confirmed.scenario: A screen-reader user (or Sasha using VoiceOver, which iOS surfaces heavily for exactly this kind of chat UI) sends a message to the coach. `state.typing` becomes true and the 'Thinking' div (which does carry `aria-live="polite"`, line 164) is announced. When the response arrives, `nextChatState`'s 'turn' case (line 60-69) sets `typing: false` — the 'Thinking' node is removed from the DOM — and appends the new assistant message into `state.messages`, which is rendered by the plain, non-live `.map()` at line 159-161. CoachMessage (components/CoachMessage.tsx) itself has no `aria-live` or `role="status"` either.
confirmed.impact: A screen-reader user gets 'Thinking' announced, then silence — the actual coach answer (which may carry an allowed/blocked verdict on a food she's about to eat) is inserted into the DOM without any live-region signal, so nothing is spoken. She would have to manually re-navigate into the transcript to discover a reply ever arrived, on a feature whose whole point is a fast back-and-forth.
confirmed.fix: Wrap the messages list (or at minimum the newly-appended assistant bubble) in a container with `aria-live="polite"` `aria-atomic="false"` so each new turn is announced the same way the transient 'Thinking' state already is.

confirmed.title: Tab bar row count jumps once Body capability resolves
confirmed.scenario: lib/health/capability-client.ts's `useBodyCapability` starts at `capability: BodyCapability = "unknown"` (line 19) and only resolves inside a `useEffect` via a `Promise.resolve().then(...)` chain (lines 22-30) — i.e. after the first paint, never synchronously. Since `tabsFor` only includes the Body tab when the capability is exactly `"enabled"` (TabBar.tsx:129-137), the very first render of the floating tab bar on every cold load renders 5 grid columns (`repeat(5, ...)`); once the probe resolves 'enabled' a re-render switches to 6 columns. Because `gridTemplateColumns` is computed from `tabs.length` on the same `<nav>` element, every existing tab (Today, Week, Foods, Settings) shifts horizontally in place — this is the floating, fixed-position primary nav she taps within the first second of opening the app.
confirmed.impact: On a phone-first PWA whose whole point is fast one-handed daily taps, the bottom nav visibly reflows under her thumb on every cold open/reload for as long as her account has Body capability enabled (an Oura or other health source connected) — a mistimed first tap can land on the wrong (shifted) tab.
confirmed.fix: Reserve the Body tab's column even while capability is 'unknown' (render a placeholder or delay the bar's first paint by one frame until the capability read from cache resolves) so the grid's column count never changes after first paint, only the tab bar's already-covered narrow-viewport glyph-only reflow is allowed to change layout.

votes.reason: Every cited mechanism checks out and no guard mitigates it. lib/health/capability-client.ts:18-31: useBodyCapability's useState is hardcoded to "unknown" (not lazily initialized from the sessionStorage cache); the actual read/probe only runs inside useEffect's Promise.resolve().then() chain, which — per React's documented passive-effect timing — always commits after the browser has already painted the first render, never synchronously with it. So even when capability.ts's sessionStorage cache already holds "enabled" from an earlier probe this session, the first paint of every TabBar mount still uses "unknown", and TabBar.tsx:129-137's tabsFor() only admits the Body tab when the value is exactly "enabled" — so first paint always renders 5 columns, then a second commit (whenever the probe/cache resolves to "enabled") renders 6, on the same <nav> whose gridTemplateColumns (TabBar.tsx:164) is repeat(tabs.length, minmax(0,1fr)) — every existing tab shifts position and every column narrows. I checked for anything that would mask this: app/globals.css's .tab-glass/.shell/.surface rules (~lines 123-214) define no transition/animation on layout properties; app/layout.tsx:40 mounts <TabBar /> directly with no Suspense/skeleton delay; tests/tabbar/flags-off.test.tsx only exercises the build-time NEXT_PUBLIC_COACH_ENABLED flag via renderToStaticMarkup and never the client-side Body-capability transition (the project's own vitest setup can't test effects at all, per the Sol audit note in docs/plans/2026-09-12-bug-batch-spec.md). That same spec (lines 378-386) documents the tri-state design intent (never render Body as on/off while "unknown") and flags that the tab-bar contract must allow five-or-six columns, but never discusses or mitigates the transient flash/reflow — so this is a real, unaddressed gap, not a scenario an existing guard prevents. confirmed.title: Oura OAuth callback rate limit uses one global key
confirmed.evidence: `await enforceRateLimit("health:oura:callback", 20, 3600);` is called with a fixed literal string, before any validation of `state`/`code` and before any identity is established (this route takes no JWT — the comment at line 2-4 says identity comes only from the oauth_states row). lib/server/ratelimit.ts:16-17 keys its in-memory window Map purely by the string passed in, with no per-caller (IP/user/token) scoping added anywhere in enforceRateLimit itself.
confirmed.scenario: Anyone who knows or scans for the path `/api/health/oura/callback` (it needs no auth header) can send 20 bare GET requests with junk or missing `state`/`code` params within an hour. Each one increments the same single counter before the state/code check runs, so the 21st request from anyone — including Sasha's own browser completing the real Oura consent redirect — gets a 429 and is bounced back to `/settings?oura=error&reason=rate_limited` for up to the rest of that hour.
confirmed.impact: The one feature that keeps her Oura ring's sleep/readiness/activity data flowing (reconnecting after a token issue, or the very first Connect Oura) can be denied by anyone hitting a predictable public URL a handful of times, with Sasha seeing only a generic rate-limited error and no way to know it was caused by unrelated traffic rather than her own actions.
confirmed.fix: Scope the callback's rate-limit key to something the caller can't spoof for free — e.g. per `state` value (which is only known to whoever Oura's real redirect carries it to) after it's read, or per source IP as a coarse fallback, rather than one process-wide bucket shared by every caller.

confirmed.title: Progress-export row cap assumes an unenforced 20-codes-per-date bound
confirmed.evidence: streamProgress computes `const cap = (opts.limit + 1) * NUTRIENT_CODES.length;` (line 298) and readProgressRows fetches cap+1 rows (lines 220-232), relying on groupTotalsByDate's "drop the last (possibly partial) date group" logic (lines 244-262). `hasMore = dates.length > opts.limit` (line 304) is computed purely from how many complete dates fit inside that capped read, not from whether more data exists beyond the last returned date. The bound of "at most 20 rows per date" comes only from daily_totals never emitting a code absent from catalog_nutrients (20260918090200_phase2_daily_totals.sql:4-7, jsonb_each(li.snapshot)), and catalog_nutrients is explicitly "filled by a worker, not a migration" (20260918090300_phase2_catalog_dri_seed.sql:1-3) — disconnected from the hand-maintained NUTRIENT_CODES literal (lib/nutrients/codes.ts:7-11) by nothing but convention. tests/export/progress-paging.test.ts only ever constructs rows with exactly one nutrient code per date (lines 10-13), so the real 20-codes-per-date shape this cap math is built for has zero test coverage.
confirmed.scenario: A future catalog import adds a 21st tracked nutrient code to catalog_nutrients without someone also updating NUTRIENT_CODES in lib/nutrients/codes.ts. Once a capped read spans a run of dates carrying 21 daily_totals rows, readProgressRows returns fewer complete dates than opts.limit even though more data exists past the last one — hasMore reads false, next_cursor comes back null, and a "download all my progress" export stops early with no error, silently, on both the JSON and CSV paths.
confirmed.impact: A plausible, low-visibility future data change (adding a nutrient the app already claims to track) would silently truncate her nutrition-progress export with no signal, and the one existing test for this code path can't catch it because it never uses more than one code per date.
confirmed.fix: Make hasMore/next_cursor depend on whether the raw read actually hit the cap+1 row ceiling (rows.length > cap) rather than on dates.length > opts.limit, decoupling truncation detection from the per-date row-count assumption; add a test using more than NUTRIENT_CODES.length rows for a single date.
confirmed.testGap: tests/export/progress-paging.test.ts only tests groupTotalsByDate with exactly one row per date; it never tests the interaction between per-date row count and NUTRIENT_CODES.length that the production cap formula depends on.

confirmed.title: Health ingest token 'shown once' copy has no failure feedback
confirmed.evidence: {issued}\n
confirmed.scenario: Sasha taps 'Issue an ingest token' to connect Health Auto Export, the sheet shows the one-time token with a 'Copy it now — it is shown once' caption, and she taps Copy. If clipboard access is denied (insecure context, permission prompt dismissed, or Safari's clipboard-write restrictions when not directly in a user gesture chain e.g. after an await), `navigator.clipboard.writeText` rejects silently; the button gives no visual confirmation either way.
confirmed.impact: The UI never tells her whether the copy actually happened. Because the token is shown once and the sheet gives no signed 'Copied' feedback, a failed copy looks identical to a successful one — she may close the sheet believing she captured the token, only to find Health Auto Export configuration fails later with no way to retrieve the original token (she must revoke and reissue).
confirmed.fix: Await the clipboard write and toggle a small 'Copied' / 'Couldn't copy — select and copy manually' status next to the code block, mirroring the pattern already used in ShareButton.tsx.

votes.evidence: components/HealthSourcesSheet.tsx:61-63 — `<button ... onClick={() => { void navigator.clipboard.writeText(issued); }}>` is a bare fire-and-forget call: no `.then`, no `.catch`, and it bypasses the component's own `run()` helper (lines 21-31) which already sets `error` state and renders it (lines 101-103). Compare components/ShareButton.tsx:31,48-51, which awaits the same API and sets a `status` of 'idle'/'copied'/'error' rendered in the button label (line 58) — the working pattern already exists one file over and simply wasn't applied here. No test file references HealthSourcesSheet (grep for the component name under *.test.*/*.spec.* returns nothing), so no guard closes this gap. The one-time-display claim is also verified: `issued` (line 15) is local component state with no persistence, and the sheet's own caption says "Copy it now — it is shown once" (line 55), confirming that once the sheet is closed the token is unrecoverable and Sasha would have to revoke and reissue.

The cited onClick handler is exactly as quoted: a void-discarded promise with no success/failure branch, while an error-display mechanism (error state, rendered at lines 101-103) already exists in this component for its other actions and is simply not wired to the Copy button. The comparison to ShareButton.tsx's status pattern is correct and shows the fix is small and already precedented in-repo, not speculative. One nuance weakens (but doesn't refute) the scenario as literally stated: this onClick fires synchronously, directly from the user gesture (no prior await), so the specific 'Safari clipboard-write restriction after an await' mechanism the finding names doesn't strictly apply to this call site — real rejection here would come from rarer causes (insecure context, revoked permission, an extension/policy blocking clipboard access), which are low-probability but not impossible. That inaccuracy is about the cause, not the defect: the observable bug (silent success/failure, no feedback, one-shot token loss requiring revoke+reissue) is real and unguarded. Given the failure trigger is narrow, it affects only a one-time device-setup flow rather than Sasha's daily meal-logging path, and it is recoverable (revoke/reissue, not data loss or a broken safety rule), 'medium' is the right severity — not high (no wrong numbers, no silent failure on a frequent/main path) and not merely low (the token really is unrecoverable once lost, and the fix is trivial and already precedented in the same codebase).

confirmed.impact: AGENTS.md's guarded rule #4 — "Any date renders a complete day; there is no start date and no end date" — and rotation.ts's own docstring promise ("Everything is a pure function of the calendar date... the same date always yields the same meal") have no test that would fail if a slot silently vanished. This is a genuine, provable defect in the test (not a style nit): it can only catch reordering or an extraneous slot, never an omission. I confirmed the underlying code path is real: `lib/foods.ts:333` (`if (P + C + F === 0) return [];` inside `rotationPool`) and `lib/rotation.ts:143` (`if (pool.length === 0) continue;` inside `mealsForDay`) together let a slot silently vanish from the resolved day, and this is reachable in production via `lib/resolve.ts:137` (`mealsForDay(date, stored, undefined, store.foods)`), which backs both the Today screen and MCP `get_day` per AGENTS.md.
