I traced `rotationPool` line by line: when only ONE role (e.g. protein) is fully avoided, P=0 but C,F>0, so `cycle = lcm(lcm(max(0,1),C),F)` is still positive and the loop still emits `n` meals with `protein: null` — the pool is NOT empty and the slot is NOT dropped (it just silently loses one macro component, a different bug from the one described). confirmed.title: Dedupe key has no type disambiguation when a source supplies its own vendor_sample_id
confirmed.scenario: When vendor_sample_id is present the effective identity of a health observation is the vendor id ALONE - type is never folded in. Only lib/oura/map.ts is careful to defend against this, by hand-crafting vendor_sample_id: `${id}:${type}` (map.ts:19) so its own samples never collide across metric types. The Shortcut ingest path (lib/health/normalize.ts:117-119, normalizeShortcut) passes through whatever vendor_sample_id the phone-side Shortcut script supplies, completely unchecked and undocumented as needing a type suffix. If that script (or any future integration reusing this same field) ever emits the same vendor_sample_id for two different sample types from the same source (e.g. sleep_asleep and sleep_in_bed derived from one exported record), the second insert collides on the unique index (user_id, source_id, dedupe_key) and lands in the on conflict do update branch, which overwrites value/unit/end_time but never updates type - so the second sample's true type is silently discarded and its numeric value is stored/labeled under the FIRST sample's type instead.
confirmed.impact: A silent cross-metric data corruption with no rejected/error signal anywhere in the response (rejected stays empty, the row is reported as updated) - e.g. a sleep-in-bed reading could silently overwrite what's stored as sleep_asleep (or vice versa), corrupting the number Sasha sees for her own sleep on the Body dashboard, with nothing in the ingest response or logs indicating anything went wrong.
confirmed.fix: Fold type into the dedupe key unconditionally, even when vendor_sample_id is present, e.g. dedupe_key = type || ':' || coalesce(vendor_sample_id, start|end) in both the TS dedupeKey() and the DB generated column, so two different metric types can never collide regardless of what a source's vendor id looks like.

confirmed.title: AI spend cap and capture daily cap are check-then-act, not atomic
confirmed.evidence: `assertUnderSpendCap` (lines 82-103) reads the sum of today's `cost_estimate` from `ai_calls` and throws only if `spent >= cap`; the provider call and the row that adds to `spent` both happen strictly after this read, inside `generateStructured` (line 299 onward). The equivalent capture-side check, `assertUnderCaps` in lib/server/capture.ts (lines 130-152), has the same shape: read `ai_calls_today`, compare to `hardCap()`, then proceed. Neither takes a lock or uses a conditional/atomic increment.
confirmed.scenario: Two concurrent requests (Sasha double-taps a capture button, or has two tabs open) that both start before either has written its `ai_calls` row will both read the same `spent`/`usedToday` value, both see themselves under the cap, and both proceed — so the day's spend or capture count can exceed `AI_DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD` / `CAPTURE_DAILY_HARD_CAP` by the number of concurrent in-flight requests.
confirmed.impact: Low real-world exposure for a single-user phone app (true concurrency is rare), and lib/ai/spend.ts's own comment frames the cap as "a brake on a runaway loop, not an invoice," so a small overshoot is within the design's stated tolerance. Still, this is the "spend caps that can be bypassed" class the audit asked about, and the overshoot is unbounded in principle under enough concurrent requests (e.g. a client-side retry storm during a provider outage, which is also when spend is likeliest to run away).
confirmed.fix: If tighter enforcement is wanted, move the cap check into the same write as the `ai_calls` insert (e.g. a Postgres function that atomically re-sums and rejects under a transaction/advisory lock) rather than a separate read-then-call. Given the current framing as a soft brake, this may be an accepted tradeoff worth documenting explicitly rather than fixing.

confirmed.title: black-translucent status bar is unreadable on the light NeuForm ground
confirmed.evidence: app/layout.tsx:13-16 sets `appleWebApp.statusBarStyle: "black-translucent"`, which per Apple's PWA meta-tag semantics renders the iOS status bar's time/battery/signal icons in white with no opaque background, letting page content show through. Every page's content starts with `paddingTop: calc(var(--safe-top) + 20px)` (e.g. app/page.tsx:111, app/foods/page.tsx:21) rather than an opaque bar, and body background is `--color-paper: #f5f5f3` (app/globals.css:24) — a near-white ground, per DESIGN.md's light NeuForm contract (DESIGN.md:4, :132).
confirmed.scenario: Sasha opens the installed PWA (standalone mode, where statusBarStyle actually applies) on any screen. The white status bar icons render directly over the `#F5F5F3` ground behind them.
confirmed.impact: Poor/near-invisible contrast for the system clock, battery and signal icons at the top of every screen in standalone mode — a native-chrome legibility issue that undercuts the 'light glass' identity the whole app is built around.
confirmed.fix: Use `statusBarStyle: "default"` (dark icons/text) to match the light ground, or add an opaque light strip behind the status-bar-inset area if translucency is wanted for another reason.
confirmed.testGap: none

confirmed.title: duplicate_groups upsert only guards the id primary key, not the (user_id, fingerprint) unique constraint two devices can race
confirmed.evidence: `create table duplicate_groups (... unique (user_id, fingerprint))` (supabase/migrations/20260911000300_sync.sql:23-27). `_sync_upsert`'s `duplicate_groups` branch (supabase/migrations/20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:269-281) only handles a collision `on conflict (id)` — there is no `on conflict (user_id, fingerprint) do nothing`/merge path. Every other tombstone-capable entity here has a client-generated random-UUID `id`, so two devices independently computing the identical fingerprint (lib/sync/fingerprint.ts is a pure function of date/slot/time-bucket/items, so two devices WILL compute the same hash for the same real-world duplicate) will each mint a different `id` for the `create` op, and the second device's insert raises an unhandled unique-constraint violation instead of being recognized as the same logical group.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha logs the same meal twice close together on two devices while both are briefly offline (e.g. phone and a second phone/tablet). Each device's client-side dedupe logic detects the same possible-duplicate pair and independently queues a `duplicate_groups` `create` op with the same fingerprint but a different random `id`. The first device's create op applies fine (rev 1). The second device's create hits the `unique (user_id, fingerprint)` constraint inside `_sync_upsert`, which is not caught anywhere in `apply_sync_op`, so the RPC call raises, `app/api/sync/ops/route.ts`'s per-op try/catch turns it into `{status:'error', message: ...}`, and the client's `parkOrRetry` (lib/sync/outbox.ts:175-185) retries the identical op up to MAX_ERROR_ATTEMPTS (3) and then parks it permanently — it will fail identically forever since the underlying uniqueness conflict never resolves on retry.
confirmed.impact: Currently unreachable in the shipped app — no client code creates `duplicate_groups` ops yet (only lib/sync/keys.ts, lib/sync/merge.ts, lib/sync/types.ts and tests reference the entity), so this cannot bite Sasha today. It is a latent defect in already-deployed, already-fully-wired sync plumbing (SQL upsert, client merge/key encoding) that will silently and permanently strand one device's duplicate-group op — with no user-facing signal beyond an inert 'Sync now' retry that keeps failing — the moment the dedupe-card feature (AGENTS.md Phase 1/2 duplicate-group UI) starts producing these ops from two devices.
confirmed.fix: Add `on conflict (user_id, fingerprint) do update set ... where duplicate_groups.user_id = p_user_id` (or a pre-check that resolves the existing group by fingerprint and reuses its id) to the `duplicate_groups` branch of `_sync_upsert`, so two devices detecting the same duplicate converge on one group instead of racing a raw constraint violation.
confirmed.testGap: No test in lib/sync/merge.test.ts, lib/sync/outbox.test.ts, or tests/rls exercises two concurrent `duplicate_groups` creates with the same fingerprint.

votes.reason: Every link in the claimed causal chain checks out against the current, effective SQL and TypeScript. (1) The unique constraint exists: `unique (user_id, fingerprint)` on `duplicate_groups` (supabase/migrations/20260911000300_sync.sql:27). (2) The `_sync_upsert` `duplicate_groups` branch only declares `on conflict (id) do update ... where duplicate_groups.user_id = p_user_id` — no `on conflict (user_id, fingerprint)` clause exists in any version of this function, including the latest effective `create or replace function _sync_upsert` in supabase/migrations/20261013090000_body_profile.sql:181-193 (same shape as the migration originally cited). A plain `on conflict (id)` target does not suppress a violation of a *different* unique constraint — Postgres still raises `unique_violation` on the second insert. (3) `apply_sync_op` (supabase/migrations/20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:399-510) has no `exception when` block, so that raise propagates out of the RPC uncaught; its advisory lock is keyed by `entity_id` (v_key), not fingerprint, so two creates with different client-generated ids never serialize against each other and both pass the `_sync_current` "not exists" check (each looked up by its own distinct id) before the second one's raw INSERT fails. (4) `app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:47-51` catches the Postgrest error per-op and returns `{status:'error', message}`. confirmed.title: Signed media upload URL is valid far longer than the 60s the app promises
confirmed.evidence: export const SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS = 60; ... (line 58) const signed = await admin.storage.from(MEDIA_BUCKET).createSignedUploadUrl(objectKey(path)); ... (line 67) return { path, uploadUrl: signed.data.signedUrl, expiresInSeconds: SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS };  -- verified against the installed SDK (node_modules/.pnpm/@supabase+storage-js@2.116.0/.../umd/supabase.js): `createSignedUploadUrl(e,n)` takes only a path and upsert option and calls POST `${url}/object/upload/sign/${path}` with no expiry parameter at all -- there is no code path that could make the returned token expire in 60 seconds. Supabase Storage's signed-upload tokens are minted server-side with a fixed multi-hour lifetime (not configurable through this client call), so SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS is never communicated to Storage and is purely a label the client is told to trust.
confirmed.scenario: Sasha's phone calls POST /api/media/sign for a photo capture. The server hands back { uploadUrl, expiresInSeconds: 60 }. The client (or any component/log/proxy that captures that URL -- e.g. a browser history entry, a crash report, a debugging proxy, or a retried request queued after a network drop) can still successfully PUT a file to that exact uploadUrl long after 60 seconds have passed -- the real token Storage issued remains valid for its own multi-hour default window. Nothing else in the sign/upload path (no separate short-lived DB check, no re-validation of elapsed time) enforces the 60s figure.
confirmed.impact: The security model documented in this file's own header comment ("a foreign path costs one string comparison and zero bytes of download") and the API contract (spec §5's '60/min... 30/min/user' framing, expiresInSeconds returned to the client) both assume a short-lived, single-use-ish upload window. In practice a captured or replayed uploadUrl remains a live write-capability into Sasha's private media bucket (under her own user_id prefix) for the full multi-hour Storage default -- roughly two orders of magnitude longer than intended. For a single-person health app this raises the blast radius of any URL leak (shared screenshot, synced browser history, proxy/log capture) well beyond what the code assumes or what its own tests are likely to check.
confirmed.fix: Either accept and document Storage's real signed-upload lifetime (drop the misleading expiresInSeconds:60 from the response, or replace it with the actual value Storage enforces), or add an explicit server-side short-lived check: record the sign time in media_objects and reject/ignore an upload whose object shows up after N seconds (the media-sweep job already visits media_objects and could tombstone/reject stale-but-uploaded objects), so the enforced window matches the one the code and its comments claim.

votes.reason:
Two independent problems with this finding.

(1) The math doesn't hold up against the design contract's own baseline. DESIGN.md:155 states the layout is "One column at 390 px with 16 px gutters" — that's the reference viewport the 44px rule was authored against, not 375px. Running the finding's own formula at 390px: 390 - 32(px-4) - 2(shell) - 16(surface p-2) - 24(6×gap-1) = 316, /7 ≈ 45.1px — comfortably at or above 44px. The finding instead picked 375px (iPhone SE/mini class), a narrower device than the contract's own stated target, and got a ~43px result — a manufactured edge case, not a violation of the stated rule at its own reference width.

(2) Even at 375px, the arithmetic likely doesn't describe what actually renders. The anchor at WeekGrid.tsx:104 carries both `tap` (globals.css:232-235, `min-width: 44px`) and `w-full`. Its grid track parent uses Tailwind's `grid-cols-7` = `repeat(7, minmax(0, 1fr))` (confirmed: app/globals.css:1 `@import "tailwindcss"`, tailwind v4, no custom grid-cols-7 override found). With an explicit `minmax(0, 1fr)` track, CSS min-width on the child is not absorbed into shrinking the item — the anchor's own `min-width: 44px` wins over `w-full`'s computed ~43px, so the actual tap target is very likely still exactly 44px (spilling ~1px past its grid cell, which is imperceptible), not a genuinely 43px hit target as the finding assumes.

Even granting the worst case — a true, unrecoverable 43px cell on one specific narrow device class — this has no path to wrong food, wrong numbers, lost data, or unauthorized access, the standard the task sets for a real finding. A mis-tap on the Week grid just opens the adjacent day's page, which immediately and visibly shows the wrong date; it is trivially and instantly correctable with a second tap, with zero consequence for Sasha's meal plan, macros, or logged data. A 1px sub-visual-threshold shortfall against a house aesthetic guideline (not a WCAG hard requirement — WCAG 2.2 AA's actual minimum is 24×24px, which this clears by a wide margin) is not a real-world safety or correctness issue for a single-user phone-first PWA.

dropped.title: Oura refresh-token CAS update ignores an unmatched (lost-race) write, so a failed rotation is silent
dropped.scenario: Two calls to accessTokenFor race for the same source near token expiry: the immediate post-connect pull in app/api/health/oura/callback/route.ts:38-42 and the 06:00 cron in app/api/jobs/oura-pull/route.ts (the cron's job_runs lock is keyed per user/day and does not cover the callback path, so the two are not mutually exclusive). Both read the same `source.oauth`, both successfully exchange it at Oura for two different new token pairs, and both then run the compare-and-swap update keyed on the OLD sealed value. Whichever update runs second matches zero rows (the value already changed) — Supabase returns no `error` for an unmatched `.eq()` filter, only an empty `data` — but the code only branches on `error`, explicitly discards `data` via `void data;`, and returns `rotated.access_token` as if the rotation persisted.
dropped.impact: The database silently keeps a refresh_token pair that is not the one the losing caller believes is current. If Oura's OAuth implementation invalidates a refresh token family on detecting reuse of an already-rotated token (a common rotation-security pattern), this can break the stored credential outright; at minimum the discarded new refresh_token is lost with no record. The failure only becomes visible later, indirectly, as an `exchange_failed` error in `job_runs` — nothing tells Sasha in the app that her Oura connection quietly stopped refreshing.
dropped.fix: Chain `.select('id').maybeSingle()` (or check row count) on the CAS update and treat a null/empty result as a lost race — retry the read-refresh-write cycle or throw a distinguishable error instead of assuming success from the mere absence of a Postgres error.
dropped.testGap: tests/health/oura-server.test.ts's "rotates the refresh token in one compare-and-swap update" test only covers the uncontended success path (its own stub always returns `{ data: { id: 's' }, error: null }`); nothing exercises the CAS update matching zero rows.

votes.reason:
The core correctness claim checks out. lib/server/oura.ts:96-100 issues `.update({oauth: sealOauth(rotated)}).eq("id", source.id).eq("oauth", source.oauth)` with no `.select()` chained, so PostgREST/Supabase sends `Prefer: return=minimal` and `data` is `null` on every call regardless of whether any row matched — a CAS miss (lost race) and a CAS hit are indistinguishable, and the code branches only on `error`, which PostgREST does not set for a zero-row update. tests/health/oura-server.test.ts:74-89 ("rotates the refresh token in one compare-and-swap update") only asserts the update was called with the right `.eq("oauth", old)` key; it stubs `eqOauth` to always resolve `{data:{id:"s"}, error:null}` and never exercises a zero-match response, so there is no guard against this hole. So the described defect is real and unguarded.

Where the finding overstates itself is severity/likelihood. The cited race (post-connect pull in app/api/health/oura/callback/route.ts:38 vs. the 06:00 cron in app/api/jobs/oura-pull/route.ts:54) needs the one-time OAuth callback to land in the same instant as the daily cron on the same source — practically unreachable for a single-person app. I found a more concrete in-process path instead: pullTwoDays (lib/server/oura.ts:113-124) runs three `ouraGet` calls concurrently via `Promise.all`, all sharing one `refresh: () => accessTokenFor(...)` callback (lib/oura/client.ts:30-34), so a 401 on 2+ of them does call accessTokenFor concurrently against the same in-memory `source.oauth`. But for that to produce a *silent* loss (vs. a loud `exchange_failed` from the losing `exchange()` call, which is what most OAuth2 rotation implementations return for reuse of an already-rotated refresh_token), Oura's server additionally has to tolerate concurrent double-use of the same refresh_token — unverified, and the finding itself hedges this as "if Oura's OAuth implementation invalidates a refresh token family... a common pattern" (speculative). Even in the worst case, the persisted (winning) token pair stays valid, so total breakage needs that same unverified family-invalidation behavior; short of that, the eventual failure does surface as `exchange_failed` in job_runs on a later pull, so it isn't invisible to the system, just not surfaced to Sasha in the UI. Given the narrow, largely provider-dependent trigger conditions and bounded worst case for a one-source, phone-first personal app, "high" overstates it — this is a real, cheaply-fixable gap (chain `.select("id").maybeSingle()` and treat a null result as a lost race) but better rated medium.

dropped.title: Global pre-auth rate-limit key lets anyone silently block every cron job
dropped.evidence: app/api/jobs/backup/route.ts:61: await enforceRateLimit("jobs:backup", 10, 3600); (then bearerOk(req) at line 62). Identical pattern in app/api/jobs/estimate/route.ts:81 (`enforceRateLimit("jobs:estimate", 10, 3600)`), app/api/jobs/media-sweep/route.ts:39 (`"jobs:media-sweep"`, 30/3600), app/api/jobs/oura-pull/route.ts:29 (`"jobs:oura-pull"`, 10/3600), app/api/jobs/weekly-proposal/route.ts:61 (`"jobs:weekly-proposal"`), app/api/jobs/weekly-review/route.ts:35 (`"jobs:weekly-review"`), and app/api/health/oura/callback/route.ts:23 (`"health:oura:callback"`, 20/3600). Every one of these calls `enforceRateLimit` with a single hardcoded string key, not one derived from the caller (IP, token, or bearer hash), and does it before the timing-safe CRON_SECRET check (or, for the Oura callback, before any identity is known at all). `enforceRateLimit` (lib/server/ratelimit.ts:26) is a simple in-memory fixed-window counter keyed by whatever string it is given, so every caller of a given route — Vercel's own cron invocation and any anonymous internet request — increments and is throttled by the exact same window.
dropped.scenario: An unauthenticated attacker sends 10 plain POSTs (no Authorization header needed, no CRON_SECRET guess required) to https://<app>/api/jobs/backup at the top of an hour. Each call increments the shared `jobs:backup` window and gets a normal 401 (since bearerOk still fails). On the 11th call the window is full, so the route returns 429 before ever reaching `bearerOk`. If Vercel's own cron fires with the correct CRON_SECRET anywhere in that same 3600-second window, its request is now also rejected 429 on the shared counter, and the backup for that calendar day never runs (backup_runs never gets a completed row). The same trick works against jobs:estimate, jobs:oura-pull, jobs:weekly-proposal, jobs:weekly-review, jobs:media-sweep, and the public Oura OAuth callback — none of these require any secret or valid state to consume the shared bucket.
dropped.impact: This is a zero-knowledge, cost-free denial of service against every one of Sasha's scheduled automations: the nightly backup of her food/health/gut-log data, the nightly TDEE estimate, the weekly target proposal and coach review, the Oura health pull, and even her ability to (re)connect Oura through the OAuth callback. For a single-person safety-critical app (ulcerative colitis diet tracking with no admin dashboard watching these jobs), a silently skipped backup or a blocked Oura reconnect is exactly the kind of failure nobody notices until data is needed and isn't there — and it requires no credential, no valid payload, and no rate-limit bypass, just a handful of plain requests to a predictable, publicly documented path.
dropped.fix: Key each pre-auth rate limit on something the caller cannot make shared with the legitimate cron/callback invocation — e.g. the trusted `x-real-ip` (as auth/callback/route.ts already does at line ~28) for the Oura callback, or a fixed key namespaced per caller for the job routes only after a lightweight, cheap-to-compute discriminator (or simply move the CRON_SECRET timing-safe compare ahead of the shared-bucket rate limit, since a 32+ byte token compare is not expensive enough to justify pre-auth throttling, and rate-limit only successfully authenticated calls per key `jobs:<name>:ok`).

Tracing enforceRateLimit's logic: the first call seeds the window (count=1) and returns unconditionally; each subsequent call increments and throws 429 once count > limit — so for limit=10 the 11th call in the window (whether from an anonymous attacker or the legitimate Vercel cron invocation with the correct CRON_SECRET) gets 429 before bearerOk ever runs, exactly as the finding describes. No IP-based or identity-based keying exists on any of these routes, and no other guard (WAF, IP allowlist, Vercel deployment protection) is present in the repo to prevent an unauthenticated caller from exhausting the shared bucket. Strongest corroboration: app/auth/callback/route.ts:19-29 shows the codebase author already identified and fixed this precise vulnerability class elsewhere — its comment explicitly states 'keying the limiter on [a spoofable header] lets an attacker rotate past enforceRateLimit entirely... grouping every such caller into one shared bucket that one heavy caller could exhaust for everybody else' and keys on the trusted x-real-ip header instead. That fix was never applied to the six job/callback routes, which still use a single hardcoded key. The scenario, mechanism, and every cited line check out.

The code claim (a hardcoded, non-caller-scoped enforceRateLimit key runs before bearerOk in these routes) is accurate, but the finding's load-bearing scenario — anchored at app/api/jobs/backup/route.ts:61, with "the backup for that calendar day never runs" as the headline harm — does not reproduce, because /api/jobs/backup is never invoked by any cron. vercel.json's crons array (repo root) lists exactly 5 jobs — media-sweep, oura-pull, estimate, weekly-proposal, weekly-review — and omits backup entirely. dropped.title: Label-food idempotency check swallows DB errors, can duplicate her custom food on retry
dropped.scenario: Sasha uses 'Type it from the label' to save a new gluten/dairy/apple-free product and commits it via `/api/log/commit`. commitLogEntry (lib/log-client.ts:122-139) retries on 5xx/408/429/network failure by queuing the same `req` to the outbox, and the outbox itself retries transport failures — the exact scenario `existingLabelRef` exists to protect against. If the idempotency check's own `log_entries`/`log_items` SELECT hits a transient DB error on that retry (rather than the commit RPC itself failing), the error is swallowed, `existingRef` comes back `null`, and `saveLabelFood` runs a second time: a second `user_foods` row and a second `food_refs` registration are created for what was meant to be one custom food.
dropped.impact: A duplicate entry appears in her food list for a food she typed in once from a label. Because allergen tags and per-100g values are entered by hand for each insert, the duplicate can silently diverge from the original (e.g. one copy gets marked Avoid after a flare, the other does not), which is exactly the kind of divergence the app's own safety tests guard against for the seeded food list but cannot see for user-entered label foods.
dropped.fix: On `entry.error` or `item.error`, throw (matching the rest of this file's error-handling convention) instead of falling through to 'no existing entry' — a failed idempotency check must abort the commit and let the client retry, not silently take the unsafe branch.
dropped.testGap: lib/server/log.test.ts exists but has no case covering `entry.error`/`item.error` inside existingLabelRef

So the orphaned row this bug can create is inert — a data-hygiene leftover in `user_foods`/`food_refs`, invisible and inert, not a safety-relevant duplicate she could see or act on. The underlying code smell is worth fixing (swap to `throw` on entry.error/item.error to match file convention), but it is not a medium-severity user-facing/safety bug as framed.

The mechanical claim reproduces exactly as described. lib/server/log.ts:204-212 (existingLabelRef) logs entry.error/item.error but still falls through to `return null` / `return ... ?? null`, so commitLabelFood (line 247) reads that as "no existing entry" and calls saveLabelFood again. Result: the "existing entry lookup failed" error is logged (verbatim per line 205) and a SECOND `user_foods` insert row is produced — confirming the swallow-then-duplicate-insert defect exactly as claimed, and confirming the inconsistency with the rest of the file's throw-on-error convention (unknownRefIssues, loadCallerProfile, refsById, activeRevisionsByFood, allergenTagsByUserFood, allergenTagsByRevision, staleRevision all `throw error`).

However, the finding's severity and "why it matters" narrative do not hold up. Because apply_sync_op is idempotent on op_id (uuid v5 of entry_id+base_rev — doc comment at log.ts:1-8), a genuine retry after a prior success returns "duplicate" and applyLogEntry's duplicate branch (log.ts ~441-446) returns the ORIGINALLY stored entry/rev — it never adopts the newly-inserted food_ref_id. So the extra user_foods/food_refs row created by the swallowed-error path is an orphan: no log_items row, no food_refs join from any real entry, ever points at it. I then verified where "her food list" and food search actually read from: components/MyFoods.tsx (Eats/Avoid list) uses lib/store.ts's local `foods` map, not Supabase; components/LogFoodSheet.tsx and RecipeFoodSearch.tsx search food-db.json + `mineAsDb(f: Food)` (also lib/store.ts), not the `user_foods` table; lib/foods/adopt-client.ts's own doc comment states outright "nothing in the app lists the normalized user_foods store"; and lib/server/export.ts only ever joins user_foods through food_refs ids that are actually referenced by real log items — an orphan is never referenced there either. So today there is no UI path, export path, or Avoid-status mechanism through which Sasha could see or act on the duplicate; the claimed "one copy gets marked Avoid, the other does not" scenario is not supported by the codebase as it stands. Net effect of the confirmed bug, today, is an invisible orphaned Supabase row on a narrow race (prior commit succeeded server-side + response lost to the client + a further transient error specifically on this one SELECT on the retry) — a real robustness/hygiene gap worth the proposed one-line fix (throw instead of swallow), but not a wrong-numbers-shown or safety-rule issue.

dropped.title: Commit-time policy re-check never evaluates category, so banned categories can't be blocked at the write gate
dropped.evidence: `evidenceForItems` (lib/server/log.ts:337-376) builds the PolicyEvidence used by `policyIssues`/`evaluatePolicy` at commit time. Line 374 hardcodes `category: null` for every item, and the comment at line 334 states this outright: "`category` and `onEatsList` are not evidence the commit path has: only `blocked` refuses, and neither `unverified` nor `allowed` change what gets written." `evaluatePolicy` (lib/policy/constraints.ts:47-52) only blocks on `banned_categories` when `e.category !== null`, so this branch can never fire from the commit path. I confirmed no Supabase trigger or RPC (grep across supabase/migrations for 'banned_categories'/'category' near apply_sync_op) enforces category either — `constraint_profiles.banned_categories` (default `{simple_sugars}`, supabase/migrations/20260911000200_user_schema.sql:142) is checked nowhere in the database layer.
dropped.scenario: Any log-commit path (a catalog search pick, a coach draft, an MCP client, or any future client of POST /api/log/commit) that supplies a `food_ref_id` for a food in a banned category (e.g. simple_sugars — the category she and the coach explicitly removed on 2026-09-09) but whose upstream UI check is skipped, stale, or wrong — exactly what the previous finding describes for the coach path — reaches `applyLogEntry`. `policyIssues` runs `evaluatePolicy` with `category: null`, the banned-category branch never triggers, and the commit succeeds and writes the log entry.
dropped.impact: `/api/log/commit` is the one write gate every logging path funnels through (contracts §9a(d), 'on every item'); AGENTS.md documents the category ban as a hand-enforced rule she and the coach rely on ('Simple sugars ... removed by the coach on 2026-09-09'). Because this gate is structurally blind to category, a banned-category food can be permanently logged with no server-side backstop if any pre-commit UI check is bypassed or has a gap — which is exactly the situation the coach draft path (finding 1) creates.
dropped.fix: Extend `evidenceForItems` to resolve each item's catalog category (join `catalog_foods`/`catalog_food_revisions` the same way allergen tags are resolved) and pass it through to `evaluatePolicy`, so `banned_categories` is enforced at the one authoritative write gate, not only at earlier, bypassable check points.

votes.reason:
The narrow code claim is accurate — lib/server/log.ts:374 does hardcode `category: null`, and evaluatePolicy (lib/policy/constraints.ts:47-52) can never take the banned-category branch from that evidence. But the finding's "high" severity rests on a scenario that cannot occur with this app's actual data, and its remediation would not fix what it claims to fix.

1) Taxonomy mismatch makes the scenario unreachable today. `constraint_profiles.banned_categories` holds app-level semantic slugs — confirmed by components/ConstraintsEditor.tsx:23 (`SUGGESTED_CATEGORIES = ["simple_sugars","raw_cruciferous","raw_leafy_greens","onion_garlic","beans"]`) and the DB default `{simple_sugars}` (supabase/migrations/20260911000200_user_schema.sql:142). But `catalog_food_revisions.category` is populated verbatim from USDA's own `food_category.csv` "description" column (scripts/import-fdc.py:477-489, confirmed against the actual imported source `~/Backups/usda/sr_legacy/food_category.csv`: values are "Sweets", "Beverages", "Baked Products", etc. — never "simple_sugars" or any of the other semantic slugs). There is no mapping step anywhere in the codebase from FDC category text to the app's semantic categories. So no catalog food_ref can ever carry `category === "simple_sugars"` — the "Any log-commit path ... for a food in a banned category (e.g. simple_sugars)" premise has no real instance to exploit.

2) This isn't uniquely a commit-path defect — it's true everywhere. lib/server/catalog.ts:233-236 (`getFoodDetail`) *does* pass the real `row.category` into `evaluatePolicy`, and lib/server/coach.ts:334/353 also thread a real `category` value through from search hits. Yet because of the taxonomy mismatch in (1), those "correctly wired" call sites never block a banned category either. So there is no "other gate that catches it" being bypassed only at commit — category-based blocking is inert end-to-end for catalog-sourced foods, by a missing-classifier gap, not a commit-specific hole.

3) The proposed fix would not close the gap it names. "Extend evidenceForItems to resolve each item's catalog category ... the same way allergen tags are resolved" would only wire in the same raw FDC text (e.g. "Sweets") that getFoodDetail already resolves — which still never equals "simple_sugars". Implementing exactly the proposed change would leave the stated safety scenario exactly as unprotected as before.

4) The commit-path scope is a documented, deliberate decision, not an unnoticed omission. The code comment at lib/server/log.ts:334 states outright that category/onEatsList are not evidence the commit path has. The contract (docs/plans/2026-09-11-phase-3-4/00-contracts.md:320, §9a(d)) and its ruling record (docs/decisions/2026-09-11-wave-3-4-rulings.md, W3-10(d)) both scope the commit re-check explicitly to allergen tags plus avoid_food_ref_ids ("gluten/dairy/apple fixtures on the commit path are a release gate"), never mentioning category. This was reviewed and ruled on ("agree"), not slipped in silently.

Net: the specific mechanics cited are real, but the "high severity, exploitable, commit-uniquely-blind" characterization is not supported — the underlying protection the finding assumes exists elsewhere (and is merely missing at commit) does not currently exist anywhere, and the fix proposed wouldn't create it. This is at most a low-priority latent-wiring note (worth flagging that a future category-classification feature would need to touch the commit gate too), not an active safety-rule bypass for Sasha today.

dropped.title: Untrusted-data delimiter stripping is case- and whitespace-sensitive
dropped.evidence: `DELIMITERS = /<<\/?untrusted-data>>/g` (lib/coach/envelope.ts:25) has no `i` flag and requires the token with no internal whitespace; `sanitizeText` (lines 28-35) applies it as-is. The adversarial corpus (lib/coach/fixtures/injection-corpus.ts) only tests the exact-case token — case `do-07` plants `<<untrusted-data>>` verbatim and expects it stripped — but no case has a differently-cased or spaced variant (e.g. `<<Untrusted-Data>>`, `<< untrusted-data >>`, `<<UNTRUSTED-DATA>>`), so this gap is untested by the 42-case corpus the canary and CI run against.
dropped.scenario: Sasha (or, per the corpus's own threat model, planted content in a food name, pref note, gut note, or ingredients text) enters `<<Untrusted-Data>>` or `<< untrusted-data >>` as part of a string that reaches `renderToolResult`/`sanitizeText`. Because the regex requires exact lowercase with no internal space, the string passes through unstripped and lands inside the actual `<<untrusted-data>>...<</untrusted-data>>` block verbatim, where an LLM — which does not parse delimiters with regex-exact case/whitespace sensitivity — has a materially better chance of reading it as a second boundary marker than the corpus's own passing tests would suggest.

dropped.scenario: The moment SUPABASE_TEST_* is exported for a real run — a developer following AGENTS.md's own `pnpm test` habit against a Supabase branch, or a future CI change that finally wires the branch env vars into the existing `pnpm test` step instead of the unused `test:integration` script — Vitest's default file-parallel workers run tests/log/cross-user.test.ts, tests/export/cross-user.test.ts, tests/sync/cross-user-http.test.ts, etc. concurrently. dropped.impact: The RLS/cross-user tests are the only backstop for Sasha's data-isolation and merge-safety guarantees (the very tests the round-1 finding notes CI never runs). dropped.fix: Either point CI's Test step (and any future SUPABASE_TEST_* wiring) at `pnpm test:integration` for the branch-gated suites specifically, or add `test: { fileParallelism: false }` — or scope it to the tests/ directory — in vitest.config.ts so `pnpm test` itself is never unsafe to run against a live branch.

dropped.scenario: Sasha eats a scanned/catalog soup, has a UC flare, and marks it Avoid the normal way (the Avoid pill on the food, same interaction pattern as the curated foods list, written to user_food_prefs.status='avoid'). Weeks later she rescans the same barcode. resolveBarcode reloads her profile fresh and onEatsList correctly comes back false, but because the soup has real (even allergen-clean) ingredient text, allergenTags is a non-null array, so evaluatePolicy skips the allergen block, skips avoid_food_ref_ids (her mark was never added there), skips the onEatsList fallback (which only triggers when allergenTags is null), and returns `allowed`. dropped.impact: This breaks the single most basic safety promise of an Avoid mark for anything reached through search or barcode scan — which, per phase status, is now the majority of what she can plausibly log (13,694 USDA foods plus any OFF product). dropped.fix: Thread a tri-state avoid signal through the policy path: have onEatsList()/toMatch() distinguish 'avoid' from 'eats'/'unknown', and have evaluatePolicy block immediately when the caller's own food-pref status is 'avoid' (in addition to the existing avoid_food_ref_ids check), independent of whether ingredient/allergen text happens to be present. (2) Impact once reached: applyWindow's .or() is combined with a separate .eq('user_id', userId) call earlier in the same query-builder chain (lib/server/export.ts:166-168), which the finding's own author concedes stays intact — chained builder calls AND together regardless of what's inside the or()-string, so there is no cross-user leak and no persisted state is touched (read-only export). For the 'silent wrong data' case, the injected text would itself have to be a second well-formed date/timestamp/uuid filter clause — a much narrower, deliberately-crafted case than 'a cursor containing a comma or parenthesis.' Given the endpoint requires an authenticated Sasha session to reach, cannot leak data, cannot corrupt stored state, and the realistic failure mode is a request-scoped error response on a code path her app never exercises, this falls short of 'medium' (wrong numbers shown / silent failure on a main path) for a single-person app with no adversarial multi-tenant threat model.

The technical claim is accurate (decodeCursor at lib/server/export.ts:77-90 checks only `typeof === "string"`, not format, unlike export-body.ts's LOCAL_DATE regex; applyWindow at :118-130 splices those fields unescaped into query.or(...)), but it fails the impact bar for a real finding on this app.

Reachability: cursor is read verbatim from a URL query param (app/api/export/route.ts:124: `cursor: url.searchParams.get("cursor") ?? undefined`) on GET /api/export, gated by requireUser(req) (route.ts:167) — only Sasha's own authenticated session can call it. In the normal product flow the only place a cursor value is ever produced is encodeCursor() from real DB columns (a Postgres DATE, a timestamptz, and a UUID — see streamMeals/streamProgress), which are already well-formed by the column type. There is no UI path or legitimate client flow that ever constructs a cursor with a comma or paren in it; triggering this requires someone to hand-craft a novel base64url JSON payload and paste it into the query string themselves.

Blast radius even if triggered: RLS plus the separate `.eq("user_id", userId)` clause (export.ts:171, :225) still scopes every row to her own account regardless of how the injected `.or()` string parses — the finding itself concedes this ("can't leak another user's data"). The endpoint is read-only (export), so there is no data-loss, no write-path corruption, and no wrong numbers shown to her in the app (this is a CSV/JSON export download, not the Today screen or a ring). Worst case is a self-inflicted broken export page (duplicate/missing rows in a file she asked to download) or an opaque 500, only reachable by deliberately malformed input to her own endpoint — not a scenario a real user, or an attacker without her session already, would hit.

Per the impact lens ("no realistic path to wrong food, wrong numbers, lost data, or unauthorized access is refuted even if technically true"), this doesn't clear the bar: no wrong food, no wrong numbers surfaced to her in the app, no data loss (read-only), no unauthorized access (RLS-scoped, same-user only). It's a legitimate defense-in-depth / input-validation-hygiene gap worth a one-line fix for consistency with export-body.ts, but not a medium-severity finding under this audit's impact standard.

dropped.title: A conflicting delete/restore op is rebased through the update-merge path and unconditionally resent, silently overwriting a newer edit
dropped.evidence: `onConflict` (lib/sync/outbox.ts:140-168) never branches on `op.kind`: for any non-NEVER_MERGED, non-SETTINGS entity it always runs `mergeEntity(op.entity, local, server, ...)` (line 162) and then `rebaseOp(wireOp(op), stripServerOwned(merged), result.current_rev)` (line 164) and re-enqueues. `rebaseOp` (lib/sync/merge.ts:123-135) only rewrites `kind: op.kind === "create" ? "update" : op.kind` — a `delete` or `restore` op keeps its kind but has its (contractually empty, see outbox.ts:44-45's comment) payload replaced by the full field-merged row. The server's `_sync_tombstone` (supabase/migrations/20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:95-131) ignores payload entirely and unconditionally sets `deleted_at`/`rev`, so the merge computed at lines 162-163 is thrown away and the delete is simply resent at the new base_rev — it always applies, regardless of what changed on the server since her `base_rev`. No test exercises a delete/restore op through `onConflict`: merge.test.ts's `rebaseOp` describe block (lib/sync/merge.test.ts:159-182) only covers `update` and the `create`→`update` kind rewrite.
dropped.scenario: Device A edits a custom food's note at rev 2 (e.g. adds "hurt on 9/12" after a bad reaction, per AGENTS.md's "nothing is deleted, avoid keeps the note" promise) and syncs it. Device B, offline since rev 1, has a queued `delete` op for the same food (base_rev 1). When B reconnects, `apply_sync_op` answers `conflict` (current rev 2 ≠ base_rev 1). `onConflict` merges fields (a no-op for the outcome, since the server ignores the payload), rebases the SAME delete op at `base_rev: 2`, and resends it — the server tombstones the row, burying A's just-added note behind `deleted_at` with no merge, no warning, and no record for Sasha that a note describing a reaction was overwritten by an unrelated device's stale delete.
dropped.impact: For a UC/allergy tracker where a food's note is the evidence for why it moved to Avoid, a stale offline delete from one device can silently erase visibility of a note another device just recorded, with zero reconciliation or notification — a genuine merge-order bug, not just wasted computation.
dropped.fix: In onConflict, branch on `op.kind`: for `delete`/`restore`, skip the field merge entirely (the payload is always empty per contract) and either (a) only resend the tombstone/restore automatically when nothing else changed since the client's own last known rev, or (b) surface the conflict to the UI (or park the op) instead of auto-resending, so a delete queued against stale data does not blindly overwrite an intervening edit.
dropped.testGap: None — add a case to lib/sync/outbox.test.ts's conflict-handling describe block that sends a `delete` op through drainOutbox and asserts what happens when the server's `current` row differs from the local mirror at conflict time.

votes.reason: The code-mechanics claims are accurate (verified by reading outbox.ts:140-168, merge.ts:123-135, and the SQL): onConflict does not branch on op.kind, rebaseOp preserves kind while swapping in the merged payload, and _sync_tombstone (20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:95-131, called at apply_sync_op:482 WITHOUT passing p_op->'payload' at all) genuinely ignores payload for delete/restore. But the concrete failure scenario the finding builds on -- 'Device A edits a custom food's note ... Device B has a queued delete op for the same food' -- cannot occur in this codebase. Two independent facts rule it out: (1) the note the finding cites lives on the `user_food_prefs` row (per AGENTS.md's Food model and confirmed by _sync_upsert's user_food_prefs column list at line 176-181), and `user_food_prefs` is NOT in the tombstone-capable entity allowlist at apply_sync_op:422-426 -- any delete/restore op targeting it returns 'unsupported' and never reaches onConflict's merge branch at all. (2) Exhaustively grepping every SyncOp-construction site in the client (lib/recipes-client.ts, lib/water-client.ts, lib/log-client.ts, lib/foods/adopt-client.ts, lib/estimator-client.ts, app/api/export/route.ts) shows the ONLY place that ever builds a kind:'delete' or kind:'restore' op is lib/favorites-client.ts:49,55 (toggleFavorite), and only for favorites_foods/favorites_recipes/favorites_meals. Those rows carry just {sort, rev, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at} -- no note field exists to lose, and _sync_tombstone's UPDATE for favorites only touches deleted_at/rev/updated_at, never sort, so even the discarded merge changes nothing observable. So while onConflict computing a field-merge for a delete/restore op that the server then ignores is real wasted work (arguably worth a small simplification), it never overwrites a newer edit or buries a note in the current codebase -- the entity that has notes is unreachable via this path, and the entity reachable via this path has nothing to lose.

I disagree only with the severity: this isn't a rare cosmetic edge case, it's a documented, Phase-0-required safety property of the sync engine (silent loss of visibility into a symptom note — exactly the kind of evidence AGENTS.md says "nothing is deleted... keeps the note so she can bring it back" is meant to protect) that fires on the ordinary two-device conflict path with no error, warning, or recovery signal to Sasha. This gap is provably not capture-specific. `searchFoods` itself hardcodes `category: null` in its own `evaluatePolicy` call for every search hit (lib/server/catalog.ts:167), and the coach's search executor has an explicit code comment admitting the same gap system-wide: "read the fields directly if a hit ever carries them, which this type does not do today" (lib/server/coach.ts:214-217). Category-based blocking is inert across the entire search/capture/coach surface, not a capture-only oversight.

Even a full fix as proposed would not block real simple-sugar catalog matches. `catalog_food_revisions.category` is populated verbatim from USDA FDC's `food_category.description` (scripts/import-fdc.py:477-489, e.g. "Sweets", "Sugars and Sweets", branded categories like "Candy") — not from the app's own `banned_categories` vocabulary (`simple_sugars`, `raw_cruciferous`, `raw_leafy_greens`, `onion_garlic`, `beans` — the `SUGGESTED_CATEGORIES` list Sasha toggles for the coach, lib/policy/constraints.ts:20). `evaluatePolicy` does a case-insensitive exact string match (constraints.ts:47-51). No mapping from FDC category text to the app's slug taxonomy exists anywhere in the repo (grep for category_map/normalizeCategory/mapCategory found none). So even after correctly plumbing a real category value through, no imported catalog food's category string would ever equal "simple_sugars" literally, and the block still would not fire — the proposed minimal fix does not solve the stated safety problem.

Sasha's actual documented protection against simple sugars is different from this mechanism: AGENTS.md records that simple sugars were removed from her seed, presets, and the curated ~470-item food DB, with `bannedReason` refusing hand-typed entries. The narrow, real exposure is the newer 13,694-item raw-USDA catalog reached only via AI capture grounding or manual catalog search — a real but much narrower and harder-to-fix gap (needs a category-taxonomy mapping layer) than "hardcoded null instead of a value already in hand."

dropped.title: Legacy getSyncStatus has an unguarded JSON.parse on its own status key
dropped.scenario: STATUS_KEY (`meal-companion:sync-status`) ends up holding a value JSON.parse cannot handle (e.g. a browser extension or a future code path writes a non-JSON string, or storage is corrupted). `getSyncStatus()` is called inside `syncNow()` at the very first line of its logic (before `syncNow`'s own try/catch begins), and `syncNow()` is invoked by `SyncBootstrap.tsx` on every mount/visibility/online/local-save event via `void syncNow().catch(() => {})`.

dropped.fix: Wrap the JSON.parse in the same try/catch pattern used elsewhere in this file (`read()`), defaulting to `{}` on a parse failure.

STATUS_KEY (meal-companion:sync-status) is written exactly once, in setStatus() at lib/sync.ts:81, via JSON.stringify({ ...current, ...patch }) — a repo-wide grep (excluding node_modules) shows no other read or write of that key anywhere. dropped.evidence: `const tracePath = ".next/server/app/api/coach/route.js.nft.json"; ... const hasExternalSdk = normal.some((file) => file.includes("@google/genai")); if (hasExternalSdk) { ...; process.exit(1); }` — the only route trace inspected is app/api/coach. But app/api/log/propose/route.ts and app/api/jobs/weekly-review/route.ts (each its own `runtime = "nodejs"` serverless function) both import lib/server/capture.ts / lib/server/coach.ts, which import lib/ai/adapter.ts's `@google/genai` — the exact dependency this script and commits #70-#72 exist to verify is bundled, not externalized.
dropped.scenario: This four-commit chain (e1d47f8, 0b09fba, ac70ffd, 0812f25) exists because Vercel's App Router bundler can externalize `@google/genai` per-function and break SDK resolution at runtime. If a future change (a route-specific experimental config, an edge-runtime opt-in, or any bundler quirk scoped to one function) externalizes the SDK only for app/api/log/propose or app/api/jobs/weekly-review while the coach route's own trace still looks fine, `pnpm build` (which runs this script) still passes, the deploy ships, and every photo/voice/label capture call — Sasha's primary way of logging food — starts throwing SDK-resolution errors in production while build reported green.
dropped.impact: The one build-time gate purpose-built to catch this exact runtime failure mode protects only the least-used AI route (coach chat) and leaves the most-used one (food capture) and the weekly-review cron completely unverified.
dropped.fix: Glob every `.next/server/app/api/**/route.js.nft.json` that corresponds to a route importing lib/ai/adapter (or simply every route.js.nft.json under app/api), and assert none of them externalizes @google/genai, instead of hardcoding the single coach path.
dropped.testGap: tests/ai/runtime-packaging.test.ts only asserts the next.config.ts setting (serverExternalPackages does not contain @google/genai) — a config-level check that would stay green even if the actual build output diverged per route, since nothing reads the other routes' .nft.json files.

votes.reason: The finding's factual premises are correct (script only reads .next/server/app/api/coach/route.js.nft.json; log/propose and weekly-review both transitively import lib/ai/adapter.ts's @google/genai via lib/server/capture.ts and lib/server/coach.ts), but the failure scenario it describes is not realistic given the actual bundling architecture, which I verified against a real, current build already present in the repo (built 2026-09-13 11:42, 4 minutes before HEAD 3ca35cb, whose only change is an unrelated .gitignore edit — so the build reflects HEAD exactly). Turbopack hoists the shared lib/ai/adapter.ts dependency into ONE common root-level chunk, `server/chunks/[root-of-the-server]__1txgdto._.js`, and all three routes' route.js entrypoints (coach, log/propose, jobs/weekly-review) reference this exact same chunk file verbatim. None of the three routes' .nft.json traces mention '@google/genai' (all consistently bundled, none externalized) — I checked all three directly. Because the SDK's bundling/externalization status lives in one shared chunk referenced identically by all three routes, and because Next.js's only mechanism for this exact failure mode (`serverExternalPackages` in next.config.ts, which is precisely what commit 0812f25 removed to fix this bug class) is a single global array with no per-route scoping, there is no known mechanism by which the SDK could be externalized for log/propose or weekly-review while the coach route's trace still looks bundled. The finding's premise of 'a route-specific experimental config... scoped to one function' does not correspond to any actual Next.js capability exercised or exposed in this codebase. The gate's narrow scope is a real but low-impact test-coverage gap (checking one route's trace as a proxy for a shared chunk that all AI-consuming routes reference), not a high-severity gap that leaves food-capture or the weekly cron actually unverified in practice today.

None of the three routes' .nft.json trace files contain the string '@google/genai' (verified directly with a node script parsing all three trace files: hasExternal=false for all three).

votes.reason:
The finding's facts check out exactly. scripts/verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs:26 hardcodes tracePath to only `.next/server/app/api/coach/route.js.nft.json`. Grepping the repo confirms exactly three route.ts files transitively import lib/ai/adapter.ts (the @google/genai import site): app/api/coach/route.ts (direct), app/api/log/propose/route.ts (via lib/server/capture.ts), and app/api/jobs/weekly-review/route.ts (via lib/server/coach.ts) -- all three declare `runtime = "nodejs"`, and I confirmed all three produce their own independent .nft.json trace files in an actual local build (.next/server/app/api/log/propose/route.js.nft.json and .../jobs/weekly-review/route.js.nft.json both exist, 116-118 files each). The gate genuinely only inspects one of the three, so the structural gap is real.

However the severity is overstated. I traced the git history of the 4-commit fix chain (e1d47f8..0812f25): the actual root cause of the original incident was the global `next.config.ts` `serverExternalPackages: ["@google/genai"]` setting (added in 0b09fba, reverted in 0812f25) -- a project-wide knob, not a per-route one. That exact regression is now independently guarded by tests/ai/runtime-packaging.test.ts, which asserts `nextConfig.serverExternalPackages` never contains "@google/genai" -- this check is route-agnostic and would catch the known failure mode regardless of which API route it affects. The coach-only .nft.json check in verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs is a second, more literal/empirical layer on top of that, and its blind spot only matters for a *novel*, route-specific bundler divergence that (a) doesn't touch the serverExternalPackages config and (b) affects log/propose or weekly-review's trace while leaving coach's trace clean -- a scenario the finding itself frames as speculative/future ("if a future change... route-specific experimental config... or bundler quirk"), not something currently reproducible or observed. I verified the current build shows zero externalization hits across all three routes today, so nothing is presently broken. This is a real missing-coverage / gate-hardening gap (the proposed fix -- glob all app/api/**/route.js.nft.json -- is correct and cheap) but it matches the rubric's "medium: missing coverage" bucket rather than "high: wrong numbers shown/silent failure on a main path," since nothing is currently wrong and the known root-cause mechanism is already independently covered by a route-agnostic test.

votes.reason: The finding correctly observes that scripts/verify-ai-runtime-trace.mjs:26 hardcodes .next/server/app/api/coach/route.js.nft.json and does not glob other routes. But the actual control that decides whether @google/genai gets bundled or externalized is the Next.js top-level `serverExternalPackages` array in next.config.ts, which applies to the whole app's nodejs-runtime build, not per-route (confirmed by git history: commit 0b09fba added `serverExternalPackages: ["@google/genai"]` app-wide to fix the original incident, then 0812f25 removed it app-wide when the fix moved to a build-time version pin baked into the bundle). tests/ai/runtime-packaging.test.ts already asserts `nextConfig.serverExternalPackages` never contains "@google/genai" -- a global, non-route-scoped guard that runs on every `pnpm test`, independent of the trace script. Every AI-invoking route (coach, log/propose via lib/server/capture.ts, jobs/weekly-review via lib/server/coach.ts) reaches @google/genai through exactly one statically-imported shared module, lib/ai/adapter.ts:47 -- there is no dynamic import, no route-level webpack/tracing override, and no known Next.js mechanism in this app (all routes pinned to `runtime = "nodejs"`) that would externalize the SDK for one route's serverless function while leaving another route's trace, built from the identical shared import, looking bundled. The 'future change scoped to one function' scenario the finding proposes has no concrete implementation path in the current config surface, and would first have to defeat the global config-level unit test. Even in the worst case the finding imagines, the failure is a loud runtime crash/500 on SDK resolution, immediately visible in Vercel logs and to the caller, not a silent wrong-numbers or data-loss outcome -- so it does not meet this codebase's own 'high' bar (wrong numbers shown, sync loss, silent failure on a main path). At most this is a cheap, low-severity hardening suggestion (widen the glob to cover app/api/log/propose and app/api/jobs/weekly-review too as defense-in-depth), not a high-severity gap with a realistic path to harming Sasha.

dropped.title: Idempotent coach-turn replay silently loses a real draft
dropped.evidence: storedTurn (lines 98-115) returns `{ ..., suggestions: [], messages, draft: null, deflected: false, toolsUsed: [], model: { provider: coachProvider(), modelId: "" } }` unconditionally whenever a message with the given messageId already exists (`if (stored) return stored;` at line 234) — it reads back only `id, role, content, seq` from coach_messages (lines 106-110), never the row's own `policy_checks`/`tool_calls` columns, and CoachDraft (lib/coach/types.ts:29-33) is never persisted anywhere at all, only the smaller CoachSuggestion-shaped policy_checks array that lacks draftId and catalogFoodRevisionId.
dropped.scenario: Sasha's phone sends a coach turn whose model call actually invokes draft_log_entry and returns a real `draft` for her to confirm, but the HTTP response is lost or times out over a flaky mobile connection before her client renders it. The PWA retries the same POST /api/coach with the same messageId (the documented idempotency key, CoachTurnRequest.messageId). storedTurn short-circuits and answers with the assistant's text again but `draft: null` and `suggestions: []` — the confirm-log card is simply gone, with no error, no flag, and no way for her to tell the retry differs from the first response.
dropped.impact: A phone-first PWA is exactly the environment where a client resubmits an idempotency-keyed request after a dropped response; this makes the coach's one write-adjacent feature (draft-and-confirm logging) silently unreliable on retry, for a user who relies on it to get her meals logged with minimal friction — she either loses the drafted meal or has to spend a fresh coach turn asking again.
dropped.fix: Persist the CoachDraft (draftId, slot, items with foodRefId/grams/catalogFoodRevisionId) alongside the assistant message row (or in a joined table) so storedTurn can reconstruct the exact same draft/suggestions/toolsUsed the original turn returned, rather than hardcoding empty placeholders.
dropped.testGap: tests/coach/integration.test.ts test 4 ('a repeated messageId returns the stored turn') only replays a turn whose original generate() response was `{kind:"final", text:"Eat rice.", suggestions:[]}` — no draft, no suggestions — so the exact loss described here is never exercised.

votes.reason:
The code-level claim about lib/server/coach.ts:98-115 is accurate in isolation — storedTurn does hardcode `draft: null, suggestions: []` and never reads back `policy_checks`, and CoachDraft is genuinely never persisted anywhere (confirmed by the executors.ts:7 comment "draft_log_entry builds a CoachDraft in memory and writes nothing (invariant 3)" and types.ts:29 "Never persisted as a log entry"). But the finding's claimed failure scenario — "the PWA retries the same POST /api/coach with the same messageId" after a dropped/timed-out response — does not occur anywhere in this codebase, so the "high, silently loses a real draft on retry" claim is not supported.

Three independent guards prevent it:
1. components/CoachChat.tsx:142 — `send()` always mints `const messageId = crypto.randomUUID()` fresh inside the function body. Every invocation (initial send, Enter key, Send button, and the "Try again" button at line 184: `onRetry={() => send(state.pendingText)}`) generates a brand-new messageId. The client never resends the original messageId, so it can never hit the `storedTurn` short-circuit for a turn it already submitted.
2. public/sw.js:77 — the service worker explicitly ignores all non-GET requests (`if (request.method !== "GET") return;`), so there is no background-sync/replay of the POST /api/coach call at the platform level, consistent with the code comment in CoachChat.tsx: "a turn is a live model call and is never queued in the outbox."
3. Even for a raw network failure (fetch throws, e.g., a dropped mobile connection before any response arrives), lib/coach-client.ts's `call()` throws `CoachError(0, "network", ...)`, and CoachChat.tsx's reducer sets `retryable: event.status === 503` — false for status 0 — so no retry affordance is even shown for exactly the "response lost in transit" case the finding describes; the user would have to retype the message by hand, which mints yet another fresh messageId.

So the only way `storedTurn`'s draft-dropping branch fires is a genuine duplicate submission of the identical messageId, which nothing in the shipped client ever does. tests/coach/integration.test.ts:157-175 (acceptance criterion 4, "a repeated messageId returns the stored turn and adds no ai_calls row") exercises the mechanism but only with a suggestion-free/draft-free model response, so it's true there's no test proving a real draft survives a replay — but that's a coverage gap in a code path the client cannot reach, not a user-facing reliability bug for Sasha. I'm downgrading rather than fully zeroing severity because the underlying storedTurn behavior is still a legitimate latent defect relative to the documented idempotency contract (spec docs/specs/phase-7-coach.md:142 even describes the duplicate case as `409 duplicate_message`, which the code doesn't implement either — it silently returns 200), so it's worth a low-priority cleanup, but it is not the high-severity "silently loses her drafted meal on a flaky connection" scenario as written.

votes.reason: The code-level claim is accurate: storedTurn (lib/server/coach.ts:98-116) does unconditionally return draft: null / suggestions: [] on a replayed messageId, and CoachDraft is genuinely never persisted anywhere (lib/coach/types.ts:29 says so explicitly: "Never persisted as a log entry"; lib/coach/executors.ts:7 calls this "invariant 3" — a deliberate design choice, not an oversight). But the finding's triggering scenario — "her client... retries the same POST /api/coach with the same messageId" after a dropped response — does not reproduce anywhere in this codebase. I traced every path that could resubmit a turn: (1) components/CoachChat.tsx's `send` callback mints `messageId = crypto.randomUUID()` fresh on every invocation, including the explicit error-banner "Try again" button (`onRetry={() => send(state.pendingText)}` at CoachChat.tsx:183, which calls `send` again and gets a brand-new UUID, not the original one); (2) lib/coach-client.ts's `postTurn`/`call` (lines 82-93) is a single bare `fetch` with no retry/backoff wrapper of any kind; (3) public/sw.js:73 (`if (request.method !== "GET") return;`) explicitly excludes POST from the service worker's cache/network strategies, and there is no Background Sync registration anywhere in the repo, so the SW never queues or replays the coach POST — matching the coach-client.ts docstring's own claim that "a turn is a live model call and is never queued in the outbox"; (4) the MCP surface (lib/mcp/coach-tools.ts) does not call runTurn or touch messageId at all. Since every real caller in this repo generates a fresh UUID per turn, no shipped code path can ever produce the "same messageId submitted twice" precondition the finding depends on — a dropped response simply ends that turn (with an error shown, or none), and any user-initiated retry is a brand-new turn with its own new draft, not a replay that erases an old one. tests/coach/run-turn.test.ts also has no case for a repeated messageId, confirming this is genuinely untested rather than guarded-and-broken. So this is best described as an unreachable/latent code smell and a test-coverage gap in a documented "idempotency key" contract, not an active high-severity data-loss bug currently reachable by Sasha's phone-first PWA.

votes.reason: The finding's premise (the PWA resubmits the same idempotency-keyed POST /api/coach after a dropped response, hitting storedTurn's message-already-exists branch) does not correspond to any real code path in this repo. The only caller of runTurn is app/api/coach/route.ts:28, whose only caller is CoachChat.tsx's send() (line 142), which mints a brand-new crypto.randomUUID() messageId on every invocation -- including the 'Try again' button (onRetry: () => send(state.pendingText)), which calls send() again and therefore also generates a fresh id, never reusing the original. The UI's retryable flag is only set true for HTTP 503 (line 75, 'retryable: event.status === 503'); a genuinely dropped/timed-out response surfaces as a network-level throw (status 0), which the reducer does not mark retryable at all -- no retry button even appears, so there is no automated or manual UI path that resends the same messageId. lib/coach-client.ts's own header comment states explicitly that a turn 'is never queued in the outbox' for offline replay, ruling out a service-worker/background-sync resend too. So storedTurn's dedup branch (lib/server/coach.ts:98-115, triggered at line 234) is real code with a real gap (it never reconstructs the CoachDraft), but it is not reachable through any client flow that exists in this codebase today -- it is unexercised defensive infrastructure, not a live failure mode. Even granting the hypothetical, the consequence is bounded: a CoachDraft is explicitly 'never persisted as a log entry: the only path to one is the Phase 4 confirm sheet' (lib/coach/types.ts:29), so no food was ever actually logged from the first (lost) response -- losing the draft on a theoretical replay would only mean the confirm-and-log card doesn't reappear, and Sasha would need to ask again, which is what she'd have to do anyway had the first response never arrived at all. That is a UX inconvenience for an edge case with no live trigger, not data loss, not a wrong number shown, not a broken safety rule, and not silent failure on an actual main path.

dropped.title: MCP get_expenditure_status hands an external agent a real kcal number during 'held' with no gate
dropped.evidence: description: "Her advisory expenditure estimate: status, TDEE in kcal, confidence and the reason string. Read-only; it can neither propose nor set a target." ... async () => json(await latestEstimate(ctx.admin, ctx.userId)), (lines 31-34) — the tool forwards the full ExpenditureResponse verbatim, including tdeeKcal which lib/expenditure.ts's estimateExpenditure sets to step7Round(priorKcal) (a real, specific number) for every 'held' outcome (lib/expenditure.ts:286,291,296,301,306), not just 'estimating'.
dropped.scenario: An agent (Devin, or a coach/automation) calls get_expenditure_status while Sasha is under-logging or hasn't weighed in enough that week (status='held', e.g. 'weigh-ins in the last 21' too low). The tool returns {"status":"held","tdeeKcal":2130,"confidence":0.41,...} with no indication in the payload's shape that tdeeKcal here is just the carried-over prior, not a fresh estimate. Every human-facing surface at least tries to hide the number behind a headline like 'Holding steady'; this JSON tool has no such gate, so an agent reading it programmatically (or a person skimming raw JSON) can treat a stale, held-over number as a live current estimate.
dropped.impact: An agent or Devin making a judgment call about Sasha's calorie needs (e.g., during a coach conversation, or deciding whether to nudge a change) can be misled into treating an unreliable, non-refreshed number as trustworthy — for someone managing a restrictive diet around a chronic GI condition, acting on a wrong 'current' TDEE is exactly the kind of silent-confident-default failure that undermines the safety intent of the held/burn_in states.
dropped.fix: Have get_expenditure_status null out tdeeKcal (and weightTrendKg) whenever status !== 'estimating', mirroring what the human UI already does by convention, or at minimum add an explicit 'stale: true' / 'basis: prior' field to the JSON so a consuming agent cannot mistake it for a fresh estimate.
dropped.testGap: No test for lib/mcp/expenditure-tools.ts asserts what get_expenditure_status returns during 'held' or 'blocked' status, so nothing pins the raw-number-passthrough behavior.

votes.reason: The finding's key premise — that "every human-facing surface at least tries to hide the number behind a headline like Holding steady" — is false, and that premise is what makes the MCP tool's lack of a gate look like a novel/isolated risk. In fact the app's primary human surfaces already show the exact same held-over tdeeKcal as a plain, unqualified number: components/TdeeLines.tsx:90-94 treats any status !== "burn_in" (which includes "held") as "learned" and renders the literal kcal figure under the label "Adaptive (from your logs and weight)"; components/BodyTodayCardLive.tsx:16-19 feeds that same adaptive line into the Today card, so BodyTodayCard.tsx:106,119-121 prints "Burns about <prior> kcal a day" via tdeeLineText with zero held/stale qualifier — on the single card Sasha actually looks at daily. Only one narrow element, EstimatorCard.tsx's estimatorHeadline() (line 47), swaps in "Holding steady" — and that same card renders TdeeLines right below it (EstimatorCard.tsx:95), so the literal number appears a few lines under the "Holding steady" headline on the very card the finding implicitly relies on as the gated example. So the MCP tool isn't diverging from an established UI safeguard; it's consistent with how the app already treats a held-over prior (a legitimate last-known number, not something withheld). Separately, the finding understates what the JSON already discloses: get_expenditure_status forwards the full ExpenditureResponse, which includes `status` ("burn_in"|"held"|"estimating"|"blocked") and `reason` alongside tdeeKcal, and the tool's own registered description says the response is "status, TDEE in kcal, confidence and the reason string" — status first. The coach's separate tool registry (lib/coach/registry.ts:61-66) documents the same data even more explicitly: "status (burn_in, held, estimating or blocked), the TDEE number when there is one" — i.e. the codebase's own established pattern for this exact data already treats status as the field a consumer reads alongside tdeeKcal, not a hidden gate that needs a new boolean. The proposed fix (null out tdeeKcal for non-estimating status) would make the MCP/agent view diverge from what Sasha's own phone shows her in the same state, which is a regression in consistency, not a safety improvement.

dropped.evidence: lib/search/gtin.ts:10-20 `toGtin14` does `const digits = (raw ?? "").replace(/\D/g, "");` then only checks digit-count (8/12/13/14) and the mod-10 check digit — it never looks at which symbology produced the text. lib/barcode/client.ts:42 declares `SCAN_FORMATS = ["EAN-8","UPC-A","UPC-E","EAN-13","ITF","Code128"]`, and Code128/ITF are general-purpose symbologies also used for coupons, loyalty/gift cards, shelf price tags and other non-GTIN labels. components/BarcodeScanSheet.tsx:87-92 builds `Reading = {text, format, at}` for every decoder result and feeds it to `acceptReading` (lib/barcode/quorum.ts:19-33), but `format` is never inspected anywhere in the pipeline — only the matched `text` string survives into `resolve(accepted)` (BarcodeScanSheet.tsx:91) and then `scanGtin({gtin: accepted, ...})` (lib/barcode/client.ts:61-83), which server-side only re-runs `normalizeGtin` (lib/server/barcode.ts:211-212).
dropped.scenario: Sasha is scanning a product and her phone's camera also has a nearby non-food Code128 barcode in frame or in view during the 150 ms polling loop — a store coupon, a loyalty-card barcode, a shelf-edge price/SKU tag, or a receipt barcode sitting on the counter. If that unrelated Code128 payload's digits (after `\D` stripping) happen to be 8/12/13/14 long with a valid mod-10 check digit — a 1-in-10 chance for arbitrary noise, and guaranteed for any real Code128-encoded GTIN — `toGtin14` accepts it as a genuine product barcode with no cross-check that it came from a food-package symbology. dropped.impact: A completely different food's nutrition and allergen data — potentially a gluten/dairy/apple-containing item marked 'allowed' because the wrong product's ingredient list looked clean — can silently stand in for the pack she actually intended to scan, with no ambiguity or error signal, since the server has no way to know the digits didn't come from an actual product GTIN symbol.
dropped.fix: Restrict SCAN_FORMATS to retail GTIN symbologies only (EAN-8/13, UPC-A/E; drop bare Code128/ITF unless GS1-128 Application-Identifier parsing is added), and thread `format` through `acceptReading`/`resolve` so a reading is only sent to `/api/foods/barcode` when it came from a symbology that actually carries a GTIN.

However, the finding's stated Impact is materially wrong, and that is the basis for refuting the claimed severity. The finding says a wrong product would "silently stand in ... with no ambiguity or error signal." That is false: app/scan/page.tsx renders BarcodeScanSheet then, on any resolved/ambiguous response, renders ScanConfirmSheet (components/ScanConfirmSheet.tsx:187-193, 229-238), which shows the matched product's full description as the sheet title, its brand as subtitle, its ingredients text, and an allergen/off-plan Badge — and requires an explicit "Log it" tap (line 233) before anything is committed via commitLogEntry. Additionally, the realistic attack surface is much narrower than portrayed: for a wrong food to actually appear (not just a 400/'not_found' from OFF/FDC), the stray Code128/ITF digit string must both pass the mod-10 check (~10% of arbitrary digit strings of the right length) AND already be a real, registered GTIN for some other actual food in OFF/FDC's catalog — an astronomically unlikely coincidence for arbitrary loyalty-card/coupon/price-tag noise. The only plausible path is a stray barcode that already legitimately encodes a *different* real product's GTIN in Code128 (e.g., a GS1-128 case label or a genuinely GTIN-based coupon code), which is uncommon in Sasha's actual use context — a single person scanning her own known pantry items at home, not a crowded retail checkout surrounded by other people's coupons/loyalty cards/shelf tags.

Given the existing confirm-before-log guard (which the finding did not account for) and the narrow, low-probability real-world path to an actual undetected mismatch, this does not clear the bar for "medium" (wrong numbers shown/silent failure on a main path) as claimed.
