The finding names one concrete trigger: the documented verification step "launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.zs.smc-backup" causing a second, concurrent instance of backup.sh to race the 03:15 run. That trigger cannot cause a race. The macOS launchctl man page states kickstart's -k flag explicitly: "If the service is already running, kill the running instance before restarting the service." So -k kills any in-flight backup.sh (and its supabase db dump child) before launchd starts the new one. This is kill-then-start, sequenced by launchd itself, not two writers running at once.

The other named trigger — "launchd's own catch-up run after the Mac was asleep at 03:15" — is also not a double-fire. A missed StartCalendarInterval firing produces one catch-up run when the Mac wakes, not two overlapping ones, and launchd tracks one running instance per Label regardless.

Even granting a hypothetical true concurrent run (e.g., someone manually invoking bash scripts/backup.sh from a second shell while the launchd job is mid-run — a real but out-of-band scenario the finding does not actually describe), the impact claim overstates what the code does. scripts/backup.sh:21-25 shows the final artifact ${OUT} is produced by exactly one atomic `cat "${OUT}.schema.tmp" "${OUT}.tmp" > "${OUT}"` per process, and a previously-completed good ${OUT} for that date is never touched until a new invocation reaches and finishes that single redirect. So a prior good dump is not incrementally clobbered by interleaving; at worst a second full run's completed output replaces it wholesale, and that new output still has to pass the >=1024-byte check at line 28-33 before the script considers itself successful. There is no code path where "one process's already-size-checked-good dump... can be silently overwritten by the other's partial or corrupt one" via the two triggers actually cited.

The underlying observation that scripts/backup.sh has no flock/pidfile (confirmed, lines 1-46, no lock primitive anywhere) is true and a reasonable defensive-hardening suggestion, but the specific high-severity, "documented verification step causes silent data loss" scenario is not supported by the tool's own documented behavior or by the script's write semantics.

The documented verification command is `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.zs.smc-backup` (scripts/install-backup-timer.sh line 23, and docs/plans/2026-09-10-phase-0/lane-D-data-ops.md:2280 shows this is meant to be run exactly once, immediately after `scripts/install-backup-timer.sh`, as a one-time post-install smoke check — not a recurring "test something" action). 2. `launchctl kickstart -k` is specifically the *kill-then-start* form: per launchd's documented semantics, if the named job is already running, `-k` sends it a kill signal first and only then starts a fresh single instance. It does not spawn a second concurrent instance alongside a still-running one — that is exactly what `-k` is for. Without `-k`, kickstart on an already-running job errors out rather than double-launching. Either way there is no window where two `supabase db dump`/`cat` writers are both live against the same `${OUT}` path from this command.

3. launchd treats a given Label as a singleton job. A `StartCalendarInterval` firing (including a post-sleep catch-up run) while a previous invocation of the same job is still executing does not start a second concurrent instance of that job — it does not double-fire concurrently. So the "manual kickstart overlapping the 03:15 interval, or a sleep catch-up run" mechanism the finding proposes does not produce the concurrent race it describes.

The only way to actually get two live writers into the same ${STAMP}.sql is to bypass launchctl entirely — e.g. run `bash scripts/backup.sh` directly from a terminal at the same moment the launchd-managed instance is independently running — which is self-inflicted, not part of any documented or intended workflow, and not what the finding's own reproduction scenario describes. That is a real but far narrower residual gap than "high, data-loss, triggered by the documented verification step."

votes.reason: All cited code facts check out verbatim: scripts/backup.sh:20-26 has no flock/pidfile, writes to date-derived fixed paths (${OUT}.tmp, ${OUT}.schema.tmp, ${OUT}), and the size guard at line 29 only runs once per process against whichever finishes last. launchd/com.zs.smc-backup.plist:11-15 confirms RunAtLoad=false and a single StartCalendarInterval(03:15) with no ThrottleInterval, and install-backup-timer.sh:22-23 does print `launchctl kickstart -k ...` as its own verification step. So the mechanism described is real. But the claimed "catch-up run after the Mac was asleep at 03:15" half of the trigger scenario is not how launchd StartCalendarInterval behaves when RunAtLoad is false and no WakeSystemForEvents/watchPaths is set -- macOS does not replay a missed calendar-interval job on wake, it just skips it -- so the only realistic double-fire path is a human deliberately re-running the printed kickstart command (or backup.sh by hand) in the same minute the 03:15 cron fires, which is an install-time/debugging action, not something that happens in Sasha's day-to-day use of the app. Even granting the race, the blast radius is bounded: this script only writes a local .sql file on Devin's own Mac under ~/Backups/supabase/meal-companion, one of 14 retained daily dumps; production Supabase data is never touched or overwritten, the app's live path (foods, meals, macros, gluten/dairy/apple flags Sasha actually sees) is completely unaffected, and AGENTS.md documents a second, independent backup path (app/api/jobs/backup, the Vercel cron JSON copy) plus 13 adjacent days of local dumps as fallback recovery material. So a successful clobber degrades one day of one of two redundant backup mechanisms -- it does not cause wrong numbers shown to Sasha, does not lose her live data, and is not a silent failure on a path she or the running app ever exercises. That falls short of this audit's "high" bar (wrong numbers shown, sync loss, silent failure on a main path) and is better characterized as a real but narrow ops-hygiene gap in a manually-triggered admin script.
